This paper investigates CF-approximation spaces, focusing on the properties of CF-open sets, CF-closed sets, and CF-continuity. We introduce the concept of CF-closed sets within these spaces and demonstrate that they correspond to closed sets in a continuous domain. Furthermore, we examine the characteristics of CF-closed sets under various operations, specifically addressing their behavior regarding unions, intersections, and complementation. Finally, we explore the properties of CF-closed-valued continuous functions defined on CF-approximation spaces.

We introduce an efficient, exact algorithm for the paired-permutation test, a statistical method used to evaluate the null hypothesis that the population mean difference between two groups is zero. While commonly approximated via Monte Carlo techniques, our approach computes the exact $p$-value by enumerating all possible outcomes under the null hypothesis. We demonstrate that the algorithm's running time scales exponentially with the number of observations in the smaller group but remains independent of the data's numerical values. Furthermore, we present a new, specialized data structure that allows the exact enumeration of the test statistic's distribution to occur far more rapidly than previous methods. This data structure is particularly advantageous when the smaller group contains a small number of elements with a large range of values. We illustrate the algorithm's utility by applying it to the paired $t$-test, calculating exact $p$-values for the two-sample $t$-test, and performing exact post-hoc pairwise comparisons following a significant Friedman test.

This study examines the dissolution of shipping cartels, utilizing a dataset of weekly freight rates and vessel volumes from 1990 to 2019. The analysis reveals that cartel disintegration occurred in two distinct stages: an initial phase between 1990 and 1999, where cartels were dismantled by regulators, and a subsequent phase from 2000 to 2004, where cartels became unviable due to deregulation. The findings indicate that both the loss of regulatory enforcement and the resulting economic unviability led to significant reductions in cartel power. This decline resulted in a 10% drop in freight rates and a corresponding 7% increase in shipping volumes. Furthermore, the study highlights that the impact of regulatory enforcement was notably more pronounced than that of economic unviability.

We introduce the concept of loom spaces, which serve as a broad generalization of both loomings and oriented matroids. For every loom space, we define an associated topological triangulation that shares the same oriented matroid as the original space; this specific triangulation is referred to as the canonical triangulation. We demonstrate that the canonical triangulation is 2-cell connected whenever the loom space is 2-cell connected, and we provide a method to explicitly construct it. Furthermore, we show that every loom space is homotopically equivalent to its canonical triangulation.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various domains, yet the reasons for their effectiveness remain unclear. While prior research suggests that GNNs may struggle with overfitting on node features but excel with graph structure, this study provides a more thorough investigation into the contributions of graph structure versus node features in GNN performance. We introduce a novel framework called GraphJigsaw, which systematically alters graph topology by rearranging node connections. Our experiments reveal that graph structure is a more significant determinant of performance than previously thought, with GraphJigsaw outperforming existing methods by a 1.5x margin. Furthermore, we present GraphSolv, a new approach that surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques by 1.5x in performance. Our findings indicate that GraphSolv effectively leverages graph topology, thereby enhancing overall GNN performance.

Adaptive input selection has become increasingly vital in dimensionality reduction, yet it has received relatively little attention. Although numerous traditional dimensionality reduction methods exist, their adaptability to input selection remains largely unexamined. This study investigates the impact of adaptive inputs on conventional dimensionality reduction approaches, revealing that even when applied to standard algorithms, adaptive input selection can significantly alter the resulting low-dimensional embedding. Furthermore, this effect often renders traditional point-estimation methods—such as the average pooling used in most existing literature—insufficient. In response, we demonstrate that incorporating stochastic elements into the input selection process enhances the robustness of these traditional estimators. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel stochastic adaptation of t-SNE, termed Stochastic t-SNE (St-SNE), which utilizes adaptive input sampling to better preserve local data structures. Empirical evaluations across both synthetic and real-world datasets indicate that St-SNE outperforms existing dimensionality reduction techniques in terms of accuracy.

We develop a series of surgery-based arguments tailored for analyzing geometries arising from singular compact area-minimizing sets. Although this work is motivated by the study of minimal hypersurfaces within a bounded 3-dimensional region, the methodologies employed are applicable to various other contexts involving singular minimal surfaces.

We report on the measurement of entropy within the cores of vortex lattices in YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_{6.95}$, utilizing a scanning SQUID microscope to determine vortex positions and a calorimeter to detect the entropy influx caused by vortex motion. The findings indicate that the entropy residing in a vortex core is significantly lower than that of a solitary flux line moving through the superconductor. This reduction is attributed to the screening of magnetic fields by neighboring vortices, which diminishes the entropy density in the core by a factor of approximately 100. Consequently, the entropy influx into a vortex lattice is reduced by roughly two orders of magnitude compared to that of an isolated vortex.

This paper addresses the challenge of coordinating a distributed collection of loads to communicate with a system operator via a centralized aggregator. We introduce Maximum Entropy Feedback (MEF), a novel strategy that empowers each load to transmit only a limited amount of data. Under MEF, every load generates a random signal drawn from a distribution determined by its current state and the observed data sent by the aggregator. This approach fostes high randomness in the information stream, thereby maximizing the long-term entropy of the feedback provided to the central system. We demonstrate that despite the inherent unpredictability of individual messages, the aggregate effect of MEF ensures the stability of the entire system. Furthermore, we show that the convergence speed of the aggregate load remains largely unaffected by the level of randomness introduced. The theoretical framework is validated through a specific application in demand response programs, where flexible loads adjust their power consumption in response to pricing signals from the aggregator.

Stock market forecasting is a critical challenge for investors, as it can significantly influence their financial outcomes. This study aims to predict short-term stock price trends by leveraging a diverse array of features, including technical indicators, historical prices, and sentiment derived from news sources. We constructed a dataset comprising 140 such features for 250 S&P 500 stocks, calculated daily from 1995 to 2017. To achieve this, we developed an automated system utilizing the `yfinance` library to compute these metrics via the `pandas` framework. Our analysis reveals that feature importance varies by stock, with technical indicators and sentiment data generally holding greater significance than raw price history. Furthermore, we created a feature selection pipeline employing Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) to identify the most impactful variables for trend forecasting. Our findings indicate that a model incorporating only 100 selected features outperforms one using all 140 features, suggesting that certain stocks rely on specific subsets of features for optimal prediction. Finally, we introduced a performance evaluation method designed to assess the effectiveness of feature selection in this context.

The merger of two helium-core white dwarfs (WDs) serves as a potential mechanism for both Type Ia supernovae and pulsational pair-instability supernovae. This study examines the merger dynamics of two helium WDs by employing the Generalized Post-Newtonian (GPPN) formalism alongside the WD equation of state. We calculate the merger timescales for various WD configurations, utilizing the GPPN approach to determine the merger orbital separation and the corresponding merger time. Our findings indicate that the merger timescales are sensitive to both the mass ratio and the radii of the WDs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the merger timescale reaches its minimum value when the mass ratio equals unity.

We examine double Higgs production via top-quark loops within the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT), utilizing the leading-order terms of the expansion in the heavy-top mass $m_t$. By employing the diagrammatic equivalence theorem, we establish a direct correspondence between the leading coefficients of the Higgs EFT and those of the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) at order $1/m_t^2$. Specifically, we derive the leading Higgs EFT coefficients for double Higgs production channels involving two, three, and four external Higgs bosons.

This work presents an overview of the "pre-non-relativistic" parametrization of the four-velocity and its application in the analytical post-Minkowskian expansion of general relativity. We demonstrate that this parametrization yields a compact, consistent expansion valid for both non-relativistic and ultra-relativistic regimes, thereby eliminating the need for separate treatments. Furthermore, we illustrate its utility in generalizing the non-relativistic energy-momentum conservation law to account for ultra-relativistic effects, such as the recoil experienced by a massive body interacting with a gravitational wave.

We examine the Einstein equations within an asymptotically anti-de Sitter spacetime featuring quadratic curvature corrections in the bulk. By quadratic curvature terms, the equations become non-local and difficult to solve directly. To address this, we decouple the Einstein equations into two sets of differential equations involving quadratic curvature terms. This method allows us to compute boundary observables efficiently, as the resulting equations are expressed solely in terms of the boundary metric. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Weyl tensor and the Cotton tensor are related by a differential operator, which implies that the non-locality introduced by the quadratic curvature terms can be eliminated.

We examine the forces acting on a cylindrical intruder moving vertically through two-dimensional granular beds at finite speeds. By analyzing the drag force components across varying driving rates, intruder dimensions, and intruder positions, we identify that the drag force exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on driving rate. Specifically, an intermediate rate minimizes the drag force, a phenomenon attributed to the balance between the intruder's weight and the vertical component of the reaction force. Furthermore, we observe a distinct transition from a steady state to a steady-state flow regime as the driving rate increases.

We utilize the semi-analytic galaxy formation model SAM to investigate the impact of ionised gas outflows on the evolution of starbursting disk galaxies. By incorporating a new model for ionising-photon-driven winds, we model the momentum injection from ionisation fronts and the associated mass loss, accounting for the effects of supernovae and stellar winds. Our results indicate that these outflows significantly influence starburst evolution and galaxy growth. Specifically, they can either terminate a starburst or reduce its peak luminosity by a factor of 2 to 5, depending on galaxy mass. Furthermore, for galaxies with masses between $10^8$ and $10^9$ M$_{\odot}$, ionised winds shorten gas depletion times by up to 50\%. This acceleration of starburst evolution leads to a steeper correlation between specific star formation rate (sSFR) and stellar mass, as well as a stiffer relation between specific star formation rate and specific star formation luminosity. Additionally, the model predicts that galaxies with masses around $10^8$ M$_{\odot}$ exhibit a hard X-ray excess of approximately 1 dex compared to predictions from starburst models that neglect such outflows.

We introduce BoAnon, a novel system designed to discover high-performing configurations for computer systems by leveraging Bayesian optimization. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on expert knowledge and manual tuning, BoAnon utilizes limited feedback from an oracle to iteratively refine its search. The system employs a Gaussian process to model the objective function and uses an acquisition function to guide the next evaluation step. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that BoAnon achieves a regret bound of $O(\sqrt{d T \ln T})$, where $d$ represents the dimensionality of the parameter space and $T$ is the total number of iterations. Empirical results on two real-world benchmarks confirm that the system successfully identifies top-tier configurations within significantly fewer evaluations than state-of-the-art methods.

This study examines the transverse momentum dependence of the triangular flow coefficient ($v_3$) derived from three- and four-particle cumulants for various species of identified hadrons in $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=2.76$ TeV Pb–Pb collisions at the LHC. Our findings indicate that $v_3$ exhibits a behavior analogous to the elliptic flow coefficient ($v_2$), specifically following the pattern $v_n \propto p_T^2$ at mid-rapidity. Furthermore, the per-particle $v_3$ is observed to be proportional to $v_2$ across all $p_T$ ranges, with the proportionality constant varying according to particle mass. These results are consistent with theoretical descriptions based on the AMPT and EPOS high-energy nuclear collision models.

This paper introduces SParQLAss, a Java-based tool designed to evaluate RDF datasets using SPARQL. It offers SPARQLAss, a novel SPARQL extension enabling the computation of quality metrics. This capability allows for the evaluation of large-scale RDF data, addressing the current lack of support for such operations in existing tools. SParQLAss features a comprehensive suite of metrics covering entity, relation, and tuple levels, along with methods to identify missing, erroneous, or extraneous RDF tuples. Furthermore, the system supports the calculation of complex measures involving multiple metrics and provides a mechanism for identifying tuples that deviate from expected values.

This study examines the application of minimum density power divergence (MDPD) estimators for independent increment and Markov processes. We establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of these estimators for both discrete- and continuous-time settings. Numerical simulations indicate that, compared to maximum likelihood estimators, MDPD estimators yield more robust results when data are contaminated, with performance varying based on the specific power divergence parameter $\alpha$.

We present a 3D hydrodynamic simulation of a shock wave propagating through a molecular cloud, designed to replicate the conditions found in active galaxies. The model tracks the evolution of the shock's structure, the cloud's morphology, and the ionization state of the gas. Our results indicate that the observed properties of ionized gas in active galaxies are largely determined by the specific ionization mechanism at work. In scenarios dominated by shock ionization, the resulting structures differ significantly from those produced by photoionization alone. Furthermore, the simulation demonstrates that shock-ionized gas exhibits a distinct [O III]/H$\beta$ ratio and a notably higher [N II]/H$\alpha$ ratio compared to gas ionized solely by photoionization.

This paper introduces Frisbee, a novel framework designed to facilitate the creation of test cases for Internet of Things (IoT) applications. By offering a standardized method to model IoT systems, Frisbee enables the representation of tests using a common language, which in turn supports the development of testing frameworks tailored to specific IoT protocols. We implemented Frisbee within the PyTest-based PyRim2 framework to create a robust suite of PyRim2 tests. Additionally, we designed a general-purpose tool that automates the analysis of execution logs to detect faults, thereby streamlining the validation process for IoT software.

The rare decays of neutral $B$ mesons into lepton-antilepton pairs, specifically the channels $B^0_s \rightarrow \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \rightarrow \mu^+\mu^-$, are characterized by their extreme rarity and the presence of substantial theoretical uncertainties. This presentation outlines the experimental techniques employed to identify these rare events, the methodologies used to constrain their branching fractions, and the insights these constraints yield regarding the underlying theoretical framework.

Training autonomous vehicles to handle diverse and unpredictable traffic scenarios remains a significant challenge. To address this, generating vast quantities of synthetic data with diverse traffic situations is essential. However, creating such data requires a scene generator that produces realistic traffic environments while allowing precise control over specific situations. SceneGen fulfills this need by leveraging a neural scene representation to synthesize high-fidelity traffic situations from rendered images. It encodes the 3D geometry and appearance of the surroundings using a sparse voxel encoding scheme, which is then decoded into a novel view via a voxel-to-view decoder network. Crucially, SceneGen populates these scenes with traffic participants through a view-dependent particle generator that utilizes sparse voxel features to determine the position, trajectory, and appearance of objects like cars and pedestrians. This approach enables the creation of diverse driving scenarios by varying elements such as weather, lighting, and road conditions. Furthermore, SceneGen supports end-to-end training for autonomous driving systems by integrating with a view reconstruction module that generates an immersive, first-person driving view from the sparse voxel encoding.

This study introduces a novel, infinite, periodic, and recursive lattice structure for the Cayley tree that admits an explicit representation via the affine Weyl group of type $\tilde{A}_2$. Leveraging this new lattice framework, we develop recursion relations to calculate the partition function of the Ising model on the Cayley tree employing the star-triangle transformation method. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the parameters of the Ising model defined on this recursive lattice maintain a one-to-one correspondence with those of a dimer model on a two-dimensional torus.

We introduce a modified version of the standard FGMRES iteration, known as F²GMRES, which incorporates an extra Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization step within each iteration to enhance the accuracy of the numerical solution. Convergence properties for this new method are analyzed, and several illustrative examples are provided to demonstrate its effectiveness.

This paper addresses two unresolved issues concerning joint ergodicity. Our findings offer a resolution to the first problem posed by Frantzikakis, Leclerc, and Leung at ICALP 2019, as well as an answer to the second question raised by Frantzikakis, Leclerc, and Leung at ICALP 2019.

We investigate the formation of dust within superbubbles generated by supernovae (SNe) in large molecular clouds, analyzing the contributions from both core-collapse and pair-instability events. Our findings indicate that dust formation in these superbubbles constitutes a significant component of the total dust budget, potentially accounting for up to 10% of the dust mass in the Milky Way. Furthermore, we demonstrate that dust formation rates are notably higher in superbubbles created by pair-instability SNe compared to those resulting from core-collapse SNe.

This study introduces LiDAR-ColorFusion, a novel framework designed to enhance far-field 3D object detection by effectively merging detection outcomes from individual lidar and RGB sources. We address the challenges posed by the disparity in detection ranges and resolution between these modalities, which often result in conflicting predictions at a distance. Our solution involves a two-stage fusion process: initially, a coarse alignment is achieved through a coarse-to-fine feature matching network that merges detection boxes from both the lidar and RGB detectors. Subsequently, a refined result is produced by a detection head that incorporates complementary features from the coarse fusion alongside original detections from each source. Experiments conducted on the nuScenes dataset demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance for far-field object detection, with a mean average precision of 0.742 at a range of 50 meters.

We propose a generative quantum machine learning model designed to learn potential energy surfaces (PES) and prepare quantum states within the corresponding PES eigenbases. This approach employs a shallow, parameterized unitary circuit to generate samples from the eigenbases of the PES. By utilizing the coherent superposition of these samples, the model constructs an approximation of the exact eigenstates associated with the PES. We validate this framework through a test case involving the one-dimensional double-well potential, demonstrating that the model achieves high training accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the model exhibits strong scalability with respect to system size.

Accurate intraoperative data is essential for registering preoperative organ models to the actual surgical site. However, noise in such data can significantly degrade registration performance. This study introduces a novel approach to enhance intraoperative data quality by leveraging the structural information of preoperative organ models. The proposed method employs a level set framework to perform active contour segmentation of the data using the organ model as an initial condition. This technique effectively removes noise while preserving critical anatomical details. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach substantially improves the performance of subsequent model registration.

This study examines conformal matter collineations within a specific class of conformally symmetric spacetimes defined by a degenerate energy-momentum tensor. These symmetries are characterized by a system of differential equations, and their degrees of freedom are determined based on the tensor's structure. In the case where the tensor is non-degenerate, the resulting degrees of freedom are 14; however, when degeneracy occurs, the degrees of freedom are reduced to 5.

We introduce a novel self-supervised learning approach for optical flow that estimates visible motion by relying on object visibility cues. This method is grounded in the assumption that visible image regions correspond to actual movement, a premise that enables it to handle severe occlusions without needing synthetic training data. Instead, the model learns from real driving video sequences using an unsupervised approach. Our framework integrates two key components: a visibility-aware warping mechanism and a visibility-guided loss function. These elements allow the system to capture motion from unobstructed areas while suppressing contributions from occluded regions. Our approach represents the first self-supervised method capable of estimating flow in scenes with significant occlusion. We evaluated our model on the KITTI and Sintel datasets using only driving video data for training. Results indicate that our approach outperforms existing self-supervised methods, surpassing even supervised baselines on the KITTI dataset.

This study introduces a novel, low-power general-purpose classifier that rivals the performance of conventional Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) while offering significantly reduced energy consumption. The suggested approach, termed the Locally Linear Neural Network (LLNN), employs a straightforward training algorithm and utilizes a linear regression method for inference. During the training phase, the model identifies the $k$ nearest neighbors for each data point and constructs a local linear model based on these $k$ points. In terms of performance, the LLNN demonstrates significantly lower power consumption than standard ANNs, while maintaining accuracy that is nearly as high.

We examine the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter within an external magnetic field using the Nambu–Jona-Lasinio model, incorporating both vector and axial-vector interactions. By applying the gap equation method, we determine how the incompressibility modulus varies with field strength. Our findings indicate that a strong magnetic field significantly alters the equation of state, causing the incompressibility modulus to increase as field strength rises. Additionally, we explore the impact of different coupling constants and the ratio of vector to axial-vector couplings on this behavior.

The notion of even-2-factorable (E2F) graphs was originally introduced by Jaeger in 1983, defined as graphs where every T-join can be transformed into an even 2-factor via symmetric difference. This paper demonstrates that the conjecture by Fournier from 1993, which posits that every connected cubic graph is E2F, is false by identifying a specific cubic graph that is not E2F. Additionally, we propose a revised conjecture suggesting that every connected cubic graph is "almost" E2F.

This paper introduces a new conjecture regarding the Bateman-Horn hypothesis as it pertains to the specific case of quadratic expressions, building upon Li's recent extension of the conjecture. By incorporating the structural properties of integer solutions to $f(n)=m^2$, this refined proposal aims to provide a more precise estimation of prime occurrences within these quadratic forms, thereby enhancing the accuracy of prime value predictions compared to the original Bateman-Horn formulation.

System call filtering is a critical technique for enhancing the security of web servers by blocking malicious calls. While effective, existing methods often struggle with applications written in interpreted languages like PHP and Python due to their reliance on dynamic reflection mechanisms. To address this, we introduce Timeloops, a solution that enforces a strict ordering on system calls to eliminate the need for reflection. Timeloops functions by filtering calls at the kernel level and maintaining a sorted timeline of permitted invocations. When an application requests a call, Timeloops either executes it if it adheres to the established order or replaces it with the earliest available call that matches the requested interface. This approach is particularly effective for stateless environments such as web servers, where the next appropriate system call can be determined without needing the application's internal state. We evaluated Timeloops against major web frameworks including Apache, PHP, and Django, demonstrating its ability to block malicious system calls while preserving application functionality.

We examine the elastic scattering of pseudo-Goldstone boson dark matter within a class of theories featuring a global $U(1)$ symmetry spontaneously broken to nothing, where interactions with Standard Model particles occur via derivative couplings. We establish that the pseudo-Goldstone nature of this dark matter significantly influences scattering cross-sections, a factor that is frequently overlooked in existing analyses. Specifically, we demonstrate that the pseudo-Goldstone character suppresses scattering off nucleons by two mechanisms: first, the scattering amplitude is inherently suppressed by a momentum factor, and second, the pseudo-Goldstone nature of the dark matter imposes an additional momentum suppression. Consequently, direct detection experiments are more effective at probing lighter dark matter masses when employing this theoretical framework.

This study introduces a novel approach to managing limited sensor fields of view (FOVs) that effectively tracks both visible and undetected targets. The methodology relies on a probabilistic model of target movement and incorporates a new concept called the "virtual FOV." This virtual FOV is defined as the area covered by the union of the actual sensor FOV and the probable locations of any target currently within it. To handle the computational challenge of modeling vast unknown regions, the approach discretizes space into a grid and employs a spatial hashing technique to store occupancy probabilities. This ensures that the algorithm's time and space complexity remain invariant regardless of the size of the unmapped space. Furthermore, the system utilizes occupancy grid maps to represent the environment outside the sensor's immediate view. Experimental results indicate that this method significantly improves the detection of targets in hidden areas compared to existing approaches, all while maintaining low computational overhead.

This work addresses the issue of controlling population extinction within a prey-predator model subject to non-local, time-dependent source terms. By first establishing an observability inequality, we demonstrate the feasibility of driving population levels down to zero through appropriate management actions. Furthermore, we derive an explicit upper bound for the required extinction time, contingent upon the magnitude of the control input.

This study introduces a novel approach to the problem of learning optimal strategies in team sports by applying Reinforcement Learning (RL) to soccer. We propose a soccer-specific Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework designed to learn policy actions within the game environment. Our methodology utilizes the ProDyM professional digital soccer simulator, which offers a realistic and lifelike virtual playing field. Within this model, the state space is defined by the spatial coordinates of all players and the ball, while the action space encompasses various in-game decisions. To address the immense complexity of these high-dimensional spaces, we employ Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG), a model-free RL algorithm capable of handling continuous control tasks. Experiments conducted on three distinct scenarios demonstrate that the agent successfully acquires a strategy prioritizing goal attempts. Furthermore, the model learns to avoid low-reward actions—such as fouling or kicking the ball out of play—unless the situation offers a higher expected return than shooting.

This study introduces a novel approach to full waveform inversion (FWI) that utilizes the time-domain energy spectrum (TDES) as its objective function. By circumventing the need for Fourier transforms, this method offers a computationally efficient and straightforward alternative to conventional frequency-domain strategies. The core mechanism involves computing the total energy within a defined time window, with the window's duration serving as a critical parameter. We demonstrate that the TDES preserves significant waveform information, thereby enabling the recovery of high-resolution subsurface structures. Furthermore, we show that the method remains robust even when employing relatively short time windows. The theoretical underpinnings of TDES are explored, and its application is validated through both synthetic and field-based examples.

This study introduces a novel all-optical diode and quasi-circulator utilizing three magnetically coupled microresonators, where light circulation is enabled by chiral interresonator coupling. This specific chirality is achieved by exciting magneto-optical effects through the interaction of evanescent fields. We demonstrate that this diode's operation is robust against fabrication imperfections and exhibits resilience to reciprocal noise. Furthermore, the device functions as a circulator, with its degree of nonreciprocity tunable via an external magnetic field.

We report on the detection of a new X-ray transient, IGR J19294+1816, which was identified during the 2019 outburst by the INTEGRAL satellite. Follow-up observations conducted with Swift, XMM-Newton, and Chandra revealed that the source is located in the Galactic disk at a distance of approximately 4.5 kpc. The X-ray spectrum exhibits a hard power-law component with a photon index of $\Gamma = 1.51 \pm 0.04$ and a column density of $N_H = (1.1 \pm 0.1) \times 10^{21} \, \text{cm}^{-2}$. Additionally, the analysis identified narrow emission lines corresponding to Fe K$\alpha$ at 6.4 keV, Fe K$\beta$ at 7.06 keV, and Si K$\alpha$ at 1.74 keV.

This study examines the noisy voter model within a one-dimensional lattice where two species compete under noisy conditions. We analyze how asymmetry in noise levels between species influences the system's dynamics, which can result in three potential outcomes: species coexistence, the dominance of one species, or the annihilation of one species. By applying a pair approximation, we contrast these findings with those from the symmetric noise scenario. Specifically, we investigate the impact of noise level disparities on the critical values associated with coexistence versus single-species dominance, as well as the rates of neutral and biased drift during inter-species competition. Additionally, we examine the effect of noise asymmetry on the effective noise level governing the neutral dynamics between species.

Sundials have been a ubiquitous timekeeping mechanism in Indonesia for centuries, yet their widespread presence has historically been overlooked by the scientific community. This study introduces a citizen science initiative designed to map sundials throughout Indonesia, capitalizing on the widespread interest in national heritage following the release of the "Wali Songo" national anthem in 2022. By leveraging the Indonesian public's heightened awareness of cultural legacy, the project aims to document sundials that remain largely unrecorded in existing literature. Furthermore, the study seeks to analyze the historical, cultural, and religious significance of these instruments within Indonesian society.

This work introduces a novel Data- and Energy-Aware 2D (DED2D) framework designed to enhance the performance of cooperative data transmission systems. In this proposed model, users simultaneously receive transmitted information and energy from multiple data senders. To achieve this, the proposed system adopts the Time-Fair Information Exchange (TFIET) protocol, which ensures that each data source maintains a fair transmission opportunity. Concurrently, the energy harvesting mechanism utilizes an Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDMA) approach to guarantee equitable energy acquisition for all users. To evaluate system performance, the paper derives the steady-state distribution of harvested energy under TEFIET. Furthermore, the authors formulate an optimization problem aimed at maximizing the total data rate within the DED2D framework. Finally, the solution to this formulation is confirmed to be solvable via a low-complexity iterative algorithm.

Recent mandates for remote work have prompted a surge in the automation of physical experimental environments, thereby creating a heightened demand for effective remote debugging tools. This paper introduces a novel, cost-effective framework designed to automate experimental manipulation and debuggability for telework scenarios. The system integrates a low-cost robotic arm with a reinforcement learning algorithm to achieve task automation. Furthermore, it enhances debugging capabilities by enabling the recording and playback of both physical apparatus actions and software environments. Validated through an extensive study involving 1,500 experiments across three distinct scientific setups, the study reveals that 90% of participants successfully debugged failures using this framework, with a mean time-on-task of 11.1 minutes.

We have developed a new computational tool designed to model the electrostatic phase plate (EPP) for use in a transmission electron microscope (TEM). This device, which enables phase-contrast imaging of biological specimens at low defocus, consists of a perforated aluminum foil situated within a high-voltage electrode assembly. Our simulation framework calculates the three-dimensional electrostatic potential and the associated electric field generated by the EPP structure. By modeling the aluminum foil as a two-dimensional surface charge distribution, we determine the phase shift imparted to an electron beam traversing the device. We further model the influence of the external electrode geometry on the electric field and the resulting probe characteristics, including probe size, current density, and astigmatism. Our results demonstrate that probe dimensions are significantly affected by the fill-factor, pixel arrangement, and operating voltage of the EPP. Additionally, we analyzed the impact of varying distances between the foil and the electrode on probe properties. Finally, we evaluated the performance of various EPP designs, with a specific focus on the P-plate.

Recent research indicates that RNN-based architectures can rival or even surpass the performance of transformers on specific natural language understanding (NLU) tasks. This study investigates the performance of various recurrent structures, including BiLSTM, Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN), and various attention mechanisms, across multiple SemEval 2017 Task 4 challenges. Our findings reveal that BiLSTM consistently achieves the highest performance on the three SemEval 2017 Task 4 challenges, while the self-attention mechanism yields the lowest performance. Furthermore, we introduce a novel multi-task learning approach for the SemEval 2017 Task 4 dataset, which integrates four distinct tasks: Semantic Textual Similarity (STS), Intent Classification, Slot Filling, and Question Answering.

Loop closure detection is a critical component of simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) systems, enabling the creation of accurate maps and robust navigation. This study introduces a novel deep learning architecture for loop closure detection that integrates an attention mechanism to enhance feature extraction and matching. Unlike traditional methods, this approach leverages the attention mechanism to dynamically prioritize relevant regions within image features, thereby improving performance in challenging, dynamic environments. Experiments conducted on both the standard and modified Oxford RobotCar datasets demonstrate that this method achieves superior results compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Cloud services are increasingly utilized to maintain the Quality of Service (QoS) for video streaming, yet the dynamic nature of cloud resources can lead to unpredictable variations in video experience. Addressing this challenge, we introduce a new framework designed to proactively mitigate QoS degradation in cloud-based video delivery systems. Our approach employs a hierarchical strategy that integrates both local and global mechanisms. Specifically, we leverage local mechanisms to detect anomalies and trigger the migration of streaming sessions to more reliable resources, while global mechanisms dynamically adjust resource allocation to optimize overall efficiency. To validate our framework, we conducted extensive experiments using a prototype system built on the OpenStack platform alongside a Netflix streaming application. The results demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in maintaining QoS.

We introduce a new framework for analyzing the thermodynamic properties of doped graphene by integrating the Dirac equation with the random phase approximation. This approach treats electron-electron interactions as a self-energy correction, which modifies the Dirac cone's slope and introduces a mass term. Our findings indicate that, contrary to conventional wisdom, the specific heat capacity in doped graphene remains linearly dependent on temperature. We demonstrate that this linear behavior persists even when the quasiparticle velocity is renormalized by interactions, provided the Fermi level is displaced from the Dirac point. Consequently, the linear thermodynamic behavior of doped graphene offers a robust foundation for interpreting experimental data regarding electronic specific heat.

We introduce MaskedSpeech, a novel framework for expressive and natural speech synthesis that introduces a new Masked Speech Loss (MSL) to learn the mapping between masked speech and target audio. This approach surpasses existing methods that rely on unmasked speech or direct waveform generation. Our experiments indicate that MSL achieves a lower reconstruction loss than these alternatives, enabling MaskedSpeech to outperform them in both objective metrics and subjective evaluations. Furthermore, we developed a new scoring system for speech expressiveness, demonstrating that our model surpasss traditional methods by effectively preserving the expressive qualities of masked speech.

This study examines the orbital stability of solitary waves within a one-dimensional anharmonic oscillator system, where the potential energy combines a harmonic term with a cubic anharmonicity. By applying the method of undetermined coefficients, we derive an explicit solution for solitary waves, revealing that their energy and momentum are governed by two independent constants. Furthermore, we establish a criterion for orbital stability by analyzing the Hessian of the Lagrangian and confirming it through direct verification of the Vakhitov-Kolokolov condition. Finally, we explore the dynamics of these waves under specific initial conditions, observing that they exhibit periodic oscillations in both position and momentum.

This study examines Bose-Einstein condensate Q-balls within theories featuring multiple stabilizing symmetries. We derive a general formalism for the Q-ball density profile by solving coupled differential equations that account for the various Q-balls present. We specifically analyze theories with two Q-balls, where the interaction between the two Q-balls is shown to be contingent upon the potential's shape. Furthermore, we determine the minimum energy for a fixed charge by utilizing the derived formalism.

We investigate the evolution of a cosmological system modeling a cyclic universe within holographic dark energy, utilizing the Granda-Oliveros infrared cutoff. Our analysis reveals that the universe's cyclic behavior is highly sensitive to this cutoff parameter. Specifically, when the parameter $\xi$ is set to 0, cyclic evolution is impossible; however, cyclic behavior emerges when $\xi$ is non-zero. Furthermore, by appropriately selecting $\xi$, we can regulate the cyclic period and ensure that the cyclic dynamics remain consistent with observational data.

This paper introduces and investigates the additive Galois module structure within wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of $\mathbb{Q}$. We demonstrate that this structure serves as a powerful invariant capable of distinguishing between many such non-isomorphic extensions. Furthermore, we establish a connection between these module structures and the Galois group's action on the associated integral canonical models of Drinfeld-Vostokov torsion fields.

This paper outlines the search for neutral long-lived particles (LLPs) that decay into two photons within the Compact Linear Collider (CLIC). We examine the sensitivity of the CLIC detector to these particles across various decay lengths and masses, utilizing a simplified model where LLPs decay exclusively into two photons. Our methodology involves re-analyzing existing $e^+e^-$ \to $\gamma\text{+missing}$ data from the International Linear Collider (ILC) White Book, with the missing energy carried by the LLP originating from pair production of supersymmetric neutralinos, vector-like fermions, or dark matter mediators. Our findings indicate that the optimal search strategy shifts significantly depending on the particle's decay length. Specifically, we employ displaced dilepton or dijet searches for short-lived scenarios, while relying on a dedicated displaced diphoton analysis for intermediate and longer distances.

The meaning of words and sentences fluctuates based on their context, a phenomenon that can either represent purposeful adaptation to changing circumstances or reflect random noise. We propose a new method to distinguish between contextual drift caused by genuine semantic change and that arising from mere variance differences. Our approach evaluates whether the variance of contextual features within one set of data significantly differs from another; if so, it suggests the observed shift is driven by variance rather than actual semantic transformation. We apply this framework to analyze contextual embeddings from Wikipedia and CommonCrawl, revealing that approximately 20% of the total drift results from variance changes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Wikipedia context distribution is more stable than that of CommonCrawl, indicating greater variance in contextual variation across the latter corpus.

We report findings from the NA64 experiment regarding the constraints on dark matter interactions with electrons, derived from null results in searches for dark matter with masses between 0.01 GeV and 0.5 GeV using an ultra-light dark sector mediator. Assuming a "dark sector" framework where dark matter consists of these ultra-light particles, our findings impose an upper limit on the dark matter-dark sector mediator coupling constant of $g \lesssim 10^{-4}$ for dark matter masses in the range of $0.01$ GeV to $0.5$ GeV. Consequently, if dark matter comprises such ultra-light species, the interaction strength with standard model particles must be significantly weaker than that observed in other NA64 limits on light dark matter. Furthermore, these results constrain the fraction of ultra-light dark matter within a mixed dark sector model, provided the coupling to the photon via the same mediator is considered.

The orderly progression of retinal neurons from the inner to outer layers is fundamental to the visual system's proper function. While the mechanisms governing neuronal migration have been extensively studied, the role of cell-cell adhesion in regulating this movement remains poorly defined. In this study, we employed a biologically grounded, agent-based computational model to simulate retinal development. By integrating empirical data on nuclear migration patterns and cell-cell adhesion properties, we investigated how these factors influence the spatial distribution of nuclei. Our simulations revealed that the migration dynamics are governed by the interplay between migration forces and adhesion, resulting in a non-uniform, position-dependent nuclei distribution. Furthermore, we demonstrated that the rate of adhesion evolution is a critical determinant of this distribution. These computational insights were subsequently validated against in vivo retinal imaging data, confirming the model's predictive capability regarding the relationship between adhesion evolution and nuclear positioning.

This study examines image reconstruction in compressed sensing, where the objective is to minimize mutual coherence within the sensing matrix. By employing a greedy algorithm, we iteratively update matrix rows to achieve this reduction. We analytically demonstrate that the proposed method guarantees a decrease in mutual coherence at every iteration. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound for the number of updates required to satisfy the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP) condition, thereby ensuring successful reconstruction. Numerical experiments confirm that this approach yields superior performance compared to existing techniques.

We present a comprehensive analysis of the collective dynamics in active systems confined to dimensions ranging from 2 to 5, explicitly addressing the intermediate regimes between 2 and 5 that are often overlooked. By integrating numerical simulations with a theoretical framework that modifies standard linearized hydrodynamics to incorporate nonlocal effects arising from finite particle size, we observe a significant divergence from conventional predictions. While pure hydrodynamic models predict that the system size scaling exponent $\alpha$ (where $L \sim N^\alpha$) should equal $1/2$ for dimensions $d \ge 4$, our results indicate that $\alpha$ increases with dimensionality, reaching approximately $0.6$ at $d=5$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the standard nonlocal hydrodynamic model fails to accurately capture the scaling behavior in these higher dimensions. Consequently, we propose an alternative nonlocal hydrodynamic model that successfully reproduces the scaling exponent $\alpha$ across all studied dimensions, including the critical transition from $d=2$ to $d=5$.

Email remains a primary communication tool for research institutions, yet security breaches can lead to the unauthorized disclosure of sensitive information. This paper introduces a new approach to automatically categorizing phishing emails by leveraging the structural patterns of natural language found within them. The proposed method utilizes a Conditional Random Field (CRF) model trained on the sequential features of email content to predict the message category. The study evaluates this technique against both phishing and legitimate emails from the UMN-1 dataset, demonstrating that the CRF-based system achieves a classification accuracy of 84.5%.

We propose a theoretical framework describing an exceptional cuprate band structure that features a four-fold degenerate, topologically protected "exceptional" van Hove singularity (vHs). This structure yields a Lifshitz transition characterized by a fourfold band touching at the Fermi level, occurring when the doping level reaches a critical value. Our model aligns with recent experimental findings in La$_{2-x}$Sr$_x$CuO$_4$ (LSCO), which indicate a Lifshitz transition at a specific hole concentration. Furthermore, our theoretical predictions regarding the electronic specific heat and Hall coefficient near this critical transition point are consistent with observed experimental data.

This study examines the detection of thermal neutrons within a Gadolinium-doped liquid scintillator using the Monte Carlo simulation framework Geant4. The simulation setup mirrors the configuration of the JUNO detector, incorporating a 20-ton active fiducial volume and a 1-meter radius of interest. Neutrons generated by a $^{252}\text{Cf}$ source were simulated across various energies, with their detection responses analyzed to determine the impact of the fiducial radius on neutron detection capabilities. The results indicate that the primary contribution of Gadolinium lies in increasing detection efficiency by capturing neutrons that would otherwise escape the fiducial volume before reaching the thermal energy threshold required for scintillation. Consequently, the utility of this material is most significant for experiments utilizing extended fiducial radii, such as JUNO, where it effectively mitigates detection losses from neutrons thermalizing outside the region of interest.
This paper presents a novel application of the minimax principle to derive an unbounded solution for a specific problem variationally.

Recent findings indicate that stars possess varying degrees of diversity, which likely influences the variety of planetary systems found around them. To investigate this phenomenon, we utilized the N-body dynamics code GADGET-3 to simulate the formation of star systems within a Milky Way-like galaxy. Our simulations demonstrate that the diversity of planetary architectures is directly linked to the range of properties observed in star systems. Specifically, we identified that stellar metallicity and the orbital eccentricity of planets around their host stars exhibit significant correlations with star system mass and the number of planets, respectively.

This study introduces a new, automated system for extracting data from Chinese Resident Identity Cards (RIC) using deep learning-driven Computer Vision and Natural Language Processing (NLP). The proposed approach achieves a 96.5% F1-score, representing a 10.5% improvement over the previous baseline. Additionally, the method is adaptable to other languages, such as English, with only minor adjustments required.

Driven quantum systems are extensively investigated due to their rich and varied dynamical behaviors. Coherent states, characterized by their robustness and simplicity, are particularly valuable for exploring these dynamics. This study introduces a novel theoretical framework for deriving the exact time-dependent evolution of coherent states under a general, time-varying Hamiltonian. By employing this method, we analyze specific driven models, including the driven Dicke and driven Bose-Hubbard systems. Our findings reveal that driven coherent states can evolve into highly entangled structures known as quantum many-body scars, a phenomenon that occurs even when the driving Hamiltonian lacks off-diagonal long-range correlations.

We present the results of a photometric survey targeting 1,400 Main Belt asteroids identified by the Pan-STARRS1 telescope, with a primary goal of detecting changes in rotation states for potentially hazardous objects. The observed asteroids were monitored for up to 1,400 days, with data analyzed using the Lomb-Scargle periodogram method. The analysis revealed rotation period changes for 14 objects, including 11 that exhibited consistently accelerated rotation. Notably, the data for 11 of these 11 objects support a model of a single sudden spin-up event, characterized by a distinct "light curve gap" preceding the acceleration. This gap duration aligns with the timescales required for the spin-up process to complete. The study also identified two objects showing decelerated rotation and one object with an ambiguous trend.
