This study examines online political dialogues within the German Twitter sphere surrounding the 2017 federal election. By analyzing a dataset of 1.1 million tweets from 14 prominent German political figures, the research investigates how community affiliation develops and shifts among followers during these events. The analysis employs a novel, multi-level Bayesian framework designed to quantify both the drivers behind community membership changes and the resulting community structures. Results indicate that community evolution is primarily influenced by the political alignment of the political figures being discussed, with the Bayesian model successfully capturing these dynamics and the overall community structure. Furthermore, the study reveals that community formation is a gradual process, with distinct shifts occurring specifically during election campaigns and the voting period.

This paper demonstrates that for any compact surface $S$, the internal $\mathrm{Isom}(S)$-orbit of any open subset $U \subset S$ remains precompact under the action of any discrete subgroup $\Gamma \leq \mathrm{Isom}(S)$, provided $\Gamma$ acts transitively on $S$'s interior. Furthermore, it establishes that if $\Gamma$ is a non-elementary Fuchsian group and $U$ is any open subset of $S$, there exists a finite collection of elements $\{\gamma_1, \dots, \gamma_k\} \subset \Gamma$ such that the orbit $\bigcup_{i=1}^k \gamma_i U$ contains an invariant hyperbolic hyperplane $\Pi \subset \widetilde{\mathbb{H}^2}$, where $\Pi$ is identified with the internal $S$ of the compactified hyperbolic plane.

We present a new M-dwarf mass-radius relation derived from the Kepler mission data, utilizing a sample of 1,303 stars with known radii and a median mass precision of 10%. This dataset was refined through the removal of binary systems and stellar contaminants, with radii adjusted using the most recent radius-radius relations and radii calibrated against the Gaia mission. The resulting relation is expressed as $R/M^{0.87}$ and achieves a 10% precision for single M-dwarfs with radii between 0.2 and 0.6 solar radii ($R_{\odot}$). This formula significantly enhances the characterization of low-mass stars and the statistical analysis of exoplanets by providing a reliable radius-to-mass conversion. Additionally, the relation serves as a robust tool for estimating the radii of white dwarfs and neutron stars, which are often identified via their gravitational wave mergers.

Line waves, characterized by propagation along a single spatial dimension, are typically observed in microwave and terahertz frequencies using metallic structures. This study demonstrates that line waves can also exist in the optical spectrum by employing a graphene sheet patterned with a periodic square lattice of square-shaped holes. The formation of these line waves arises from the interplay between graphene's tunable properties and the geometric arrangement of the unit cell. Specifically, tuning the Fermi level allows the system to reach a state where the light's wave vector aligns with one of the material's anisotropic effective masses, while its value exceeds half of the corresponding reciprocal lattice vector. Consequently, propagation ceases along the axis associated with the higher effective mass, restricting line wave travel to the orthogonal axis. The width of these line waves can be adjusted by varying the Fermi level, whereas their overall behavior is primarily dictated by the unit cell's geometry.

We introduce a new algorithm that determines both the tractability and tractability for queries involving self-joins. This algorithm is applicable to queries where the mapping of variables to tables is fixed, and it generalizes the work of Marx and Pichler (2018), who handled queries without self-joins. Our approach identifies the exact characterizing conditions for this class of queries, providing both as sufficient and necessary criteria for their tractability. These conditions are verified in polynomial time. Additionally, we establish that no other characterization exists in the same sense, even when the table assignment remains fixed.

We determine the decision problem concerning the continuity of rational functions over ordered rings. Our approach relies on a novel formulation of Tarski's quantifier elimination algorithm, which incorporates partial function operations and treats them as such. We demonstrate that deciding rational function continuity is PSPACE-complete, whereas determining whether a rational function is continuous at a specific point is also PSPACE-complete.

This study presents an updated measurement of longitudinal polarization in the decay $B^0 \to K^{*0}(\to K^{\pm}\pi^{\mp})\gamma$ using $3.0\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ of $pp$ collision data collected at $\sqrt{s}=7\,\text{TeV}$ by the LHCb experiment. The analysis employs the longitudinal angular distribution of the $K^{*0}$ decay products to determine the polarization fraction, yielding $\mathcal{P}_L = (1.3 \pm 0.4\text{(stat)} \pm 0.1\text{(syst)})\%$. Comparing this result with the longitudinal polarization fraction measured in $B_s^0 \to K^{*0}_{S}\gamma$ allows for the determination of the transverse amplitude relative to the longitudinal one, expressed as $|\mathcal{A}_T/\mathcal{A}_L| = 0.014 \pm 0.004\text{(stat)} \pm 0.001\text{(syst)}$.

Reservoir computing has emerged as a powerful tool for addressing complex systems characterized by rich nonlinearities and diverse temporal scales, yet its ability to handle coexisting dynamical states remains largely unexplored. This study demonstrates that Reservoir Computing can successfully predict the evolution of a paradigmatic example of multistability—the Rössler system. We evaluate performance across various prediction tasks, including forecasting single attractors, switching between multistable states, and generating sequences of multistable behavior. Our findings indicate that optimal results are achieved when the system's natural dynamics align with the intrinsic timescales of the reservoir. Furthermore, we examine the impact of different input masking strategies, revealing that masking specific components of the system's state vector can enhance prediction accuracy.

We propose a new estimator for the $\mu$-parameter in the context of bias-reduced estimation that avoids requiring smoothness assumptions, addressing a key limitation of existing methods which rely on such bias to achieve performance. By utilizing a non-parametric approach, our method achieves asymptotic efficiency under broader conditions. Furthermore, we demonstrate through a Monte Carlo study that this estimator performs comparably to current state-of-the-art bias-reduced techniques.

This study examines the application of feedback control in determining reachable state sets within bounded time intervals for non-linear control systems. We introduce a novel algorithm that utilizes a tree-based feedback control scheme to iteratively refine reachable regions over time. Our approach is validated through a comparison with established methods, demonstrating that the proposed feedback algorithm achieves comparable computational performance while significantly enhancing precision.

We propose a novel local-functional representation designed to capture the low-dimensional structures inherent in functional data. By approximating functions as smooth segments of parametric forms, this approach offers a flexible and powerful framework for modeling data with limited degrees of freedom. We demonstrate that this method significantly improves generalization on low-dimensional signals by employing a sparse estimation technique that selects only a limited number of segments. Furthermore, we introduce a novel distance metric tailored to this local-functional representation to quantify dissimilarities between functions. Experiments conducted on both simulated and real-world data illustrate the effectiveness of our approach in enhancing predictive performance.

Humans possess an innate tendency to perceive animate entities, ranging from living organisms to self-propelled objects, as possessing agency. While prior research has examined visual cues for agency and animacy largely in isolation, this study investigates their interaction within a shared continuum. We introduce a novel experimental task utilizing a two-alternative forced-choice paradigm, where participants indicate which of two side-by-side images appears more animate. Results indicate that both visual categorizability and agency function as independent dimensions influencing the perception of animacy. Furthermore, the study reveals that the relative weight assigned to these dimensions is modulated by the specific type of inanimate object presented.

We establish a quantitative bound for the likelihood that an $L$-function associated with automorphic representations exhibits a zero repulsion near $\frac{1}{2}$, given the presence of a Landau-Siegel zero for another such $L$-function. This finding offers an enhanced version of the classical effective Chebotarev density theorem, specifically tailored to the context of $L$-functions.

This paper introduces a novel framework for reasoning about the input-output behavior of classical programs, termed Quantum Relational Hoare Logic (QRHL). This system extends the relational logic originally proposed by O'Hearn and Yang (POPL 2013) by incorporating quantum mechanics. In QRHL, program behaviors are evaluated using quantum states as proxies for probability distributions, with program correctness determined by the fidelity between input and output states. We establish the soundness of QRHL across a wide range of programming languages, including those supporting deterministic and randomized commands, as well as those utilizing classical and quantum variables, arrays, pointers, and concurrency. Furthermore, we introduce qHoareQuant, an enhanced quantum variant of HoareQuant that employs unitary operations to reason about quantum computations. Finally, we present a soundness theorem for qHoant that accommodates both classical and quantum invariants.

While standard epidemiological models typically assume infection transmission is driven by the average contact rate, the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has highlighted the critical role of super-spreader events. This study presents a stochastic SIR model incorporating Poisson-distributed transmission events to simulate the impact of these outliers. We compare stochastic outcomes against deterministic predictions, revealing that while the model accurately captures the general decline in the susceptible population, it significantly improves the representation of individual trajectories, particularly regarding the timing of infections and the final size of outbreaks. Furthermore, this approach allows for the assessment of individual risk and the probability of large-scale outbreaks. Using SARS-CoV-2 data, we demonstrate that transmission events occur at a rate 1.5 times higher than contact rates, with a distribution parameter $\kappa \approx 0.16$. Finally, we apply this framework to an enclosed setting—a crowded bar—to simulate infection dynamics, illustrating how super-spreading dynamics differ markedly from those predicted by standard models.

This paper introduces the notion of codiskcyclicity for $C_0$-semigroups of operators and investigates its fundamental characteristics. We demonstrate that a $C_0$-semigroup is codiskcyclic if and only if its generator possesses an eigenvalue with imaginary multiplicity equal to one. Furthermore, we examine the connection between codiskcyclic semigroups and those exhibiting polynomial growth.

Accurately determining the filling fraction of magnetic flux is essential for correctly evaluating magnetic field strength in maps of vector magnetic fields. We introduce a straightforward method to calculate this filling fraction by utilizing the ratio of magnetized to total plasma in the line-of-sight direction. This calculation relies on the Doppler shift and the width of the spectral line at half-maximum intensity. We applied this approach to the SDO/HMI vector magnetic field map to derive the magnetized fraction for each pixel. Our results indicate that incorporating the explicit filling fraction significantly enhances the accuracy of magnetic field assessments, particularly for fields with low magnetization.

We have analyzed the spatial distribution of 1,000 young star clusters (ages < 100 Myr) within the Milky Way, utilizing the Cluster Catalog from the HSC Survey. Our findings indicate that the two-dimensional surface density follows a power-law distribution with a slope of $\alpha \approx 1.5$. Furthermore, we examined the relationship between a cluster's age and its surface density, revealing that younger clusters are significantly more numerous and compact. Quantitatively, the surface density decreases by a factor of approximately 100 for every doubling of age.

This work proposes a new method to calculate the decay width of unstable particles within lattice QCD, specifically targeting scenarios where the particle's lifetime is comparable to or shorter than the lattice's temporal extent. The approach utilizes the Euclidean two-point correlation function of interpolating operators coupled with the Euclidean one-point correlation function of the operator coupled with the decay operator. A key feature of this technique is its ability to determine decay width by fitting data to a single exponential function, thereby circumventing the need for larger lattice volumes typically required to manage finite-volume effects. Consequently, this method is expected to significantly reduce systematic errors in future calculations of the decay width for particles with short lifetimes.

We introduce a novel class of bijective transformations utilizing complex-valued affine coupling layers, which are designed to streamline Monte Carlo estimation of complex Gaussian integrals that arise in computing Gaussian process marginal likelihoods and related tasks. These layers generate samples from specified Gaussian distributions by first applying a Cholesky decomposition to the covariance matrix and then executing sequential bijective transformations on independent standard normal inputs. We formally prove that our proposed four-step procedure yields samples adhering to the target Gaussian distribution and further establish that repeating this process with adjusted covariance matrices allows for the exact computation of integrals involving Gaussian functions. Numerical experiments demonstrate that this approach is significantly more efficient than existing methods for these calculations.

Under the Riemann Hypothesis, we present an asymptotic formula for $\rho\left(\frac{\log x}{\log y}\right)$, where $\rho(u)$ denotes the count of integers $n \leq x$ that are $y$-friable (meaning all prime factors of $n$ do not exceed $u$). This formula holds uniformly for $y \in [x^{1/2}, x^{1-\epsilon}]$. As a consequence, we derive new asymptotic formulas for the second moment of the error term in the Landau-Ramanujan asymptotic, which approximates the count of square-full integers up to $x$, again assuming the Riemann Hypothesis.

Let $X$ be a subshift within a compact, totally disconnected group $G$, and let $\sigma_X$ represent its stabilizer. We define the topological entropy of $X$ relative to $\sigma_X$ as the topological entropy of the group action on $X$ generated by $\sigma_X$. Our findings demonstrate that applying a recognizable morphism to $X$ results in an equivalent transformation, with the added result that the topological entropy remains invariant. Furthermore, we establish that the stabilizers of all subshifts of finite type located inside $X$ are generated by finitely many recognizable morphisms.

Pre-training large language models (LLMs) on massive text corpora has proven highly effective, yet current methods are largely confined to supervised learning. This limitation is problematic because the primary advantage of LLMs lies in their ability to solve tasks using only a small amount of data. This paper introduces ReCross, a novel unsupervised technique that enhances model performance by leveraging its own outputs. The method functions in two stages: first, it generates diverse samples by repeatedly applying stochastic decoding, and second, it constructs a pseudo-label for each sample by aggregating these variations. We demonstrate that ReTraining on these generated pseudo-labels significantly improves results across multiple benchmarks, including natural language inference, multiple-choice tasks, and open-ended generation. Furthermore, we show that ReCross remains effective even when using pseudo-labels from a single iteration of stochastic decoding.

This study introduces a novel distance metric called m-ar-K, designed to address dimensionality reduction challenges. Unlike traditional methods, this approach incorporates kernel functions to map data into a higher-dimensional space, thereby enhancing the separation of classes. By utilizing this metric within Kernel Spectral Embedding (KSE), we develop a new algorithm known as Kernel Spectral Embedding with m-ar-K Distance (KSE-maRd). This technique achieves superior clustering performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we propose a new criterion for selecting the parameter $m$ in the m-ar-K function, which has been validated through various numerical experiments.

This study explores the emerging field of requirements engineering (RE) within the gaming sector, reviewing current research, identifying open challenges, and proposing future research avenues. Although RE in the gaming domain is still in its infancy, the increasing availability of relevant publications allows for a comprehensive survey. By examining the definitions of "games" and "software requirements engineering" found in the literature, we mapped the scope of existing research. Additionally, we categorized RE activities specific to the domain by analyzing the terminology used in these publications. Our analysis reveals that, despite the nascent stage of this field, there is a significant concentration of studies on functional requirements. Consequently, we outline several specific areas for future investigation, including the development of ontologies, the creation of automated verification tools, and the study of non-functional requirements within software games.

Hyperparameter tuning is vital for optimizing machine learning models, yet existing methods like grid search are ill-suited for processes involving private data due to their excessive communication overhead and the necessity of executing multiple joint training runs. To address this limitation, we introduce a secure method for tuning hyperparameters that operates within a federated learning framework. Our approach allows all relevant hyperparameters to be encrypted on the client side, enabling the server to securely train the model for each parameter combination without ever seeing the plaintext values. Furthermore, the server can determine the best-performing configuration based on the model's results while still keeping the data private. We validate our method through various experiments, demonstrating that it achieves comparable accuracy to standard grid search while significantly reducing communication costs.

This work offers a novel geometric proof demonstrating that the count of spheres within the geometric realization of the Tits translation model equals the cardinality of the minimal generating set for a Coxeter group $W$. Furthermore, it introduces a new geometric construction for the folding map from $W$'s Cayley graph onto a $k$-dimensional orthant, where $k$ denotes the Coxeter group's virtual rank. As a consequence, the previously established isometric embedding of the Cayley graph into Euclidean space is utilized to provide a fresh derivation of the geometric spherical model.

We introduce a straightforward and effective method for estimating fluxes from time-series data by accounting for correlated noise. This approach is applicable to both stationary and non-stationary power spectral densities. By utilizing a simple parametric model to fit the noise structure, we derive the optimal linear estimator for the signal of interest. We demonstrate through simulations that this technique substantially improves the accuracy of flux measurements when noise correlations are present. Furthermore, we show that this method yields significant enhancements for the detection of periodic signals in scenarios where traditional methods fail due to noise correlation.

The analysis of residual abundances serves as a vital tool for identifying chemically unique stars and discerning the characteristics of specific stellar groups. This study examines the behavior of residuals across multiple elements in both the globular cluster NGC 6399 and the field star system GJ 369. For NGC 6399, residuals were computed by subtracting linear trends of abundance versus [Fe/H] and versus [Fe/H] and log(g), revealing that most elements align with these trends, with the notable exception of Yttrium (Y), which displays significant scatter. In contrast, for GJ 369, residuals were determined by removing trends relative to [Fe/H], [Fe/H] and log(g), and [Fe/H] and [Ni/Fe]. Results indicate that Y and Europium (Eu) exhibit substantial scatter when adjusted for iron abundance and/or Ni-Fe ratios, whereas other elements remain consistent with these trends. This finding suggests that Y and Eu in GJ 369 possess distinct origins compared to the surrounding population. Furthermore, the study concludes that residual analysis functions as a robust method for uncovering stars with unusual chemical compositions.

Rumors are often preceded by specific features that can be exploited to predict their growth, yet the influence of these signals on rumor metrics like peak and attenuation times remains unclear. This study introduces a novel approach that utilizes the interaction between precursor features and location data to forecast a rumor's maximum reach and rate of decline. We define the rumor growth rate as the difference in the arrival times of these features at their respective locations. By aggregating this growth rate data across multiple sources, we can accurately estimate the peak and attenuation coefficients. Our findings indicate that this method is more effective than models relying solely on feature arrival times. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this technique can anticipate the growth trajectory of emerging rumors, such as those surrounding the COVID-19 pandemic.

We derive the distance to the Fornax cluster by analyzing the spatial distribution of planetary nebulae (PN) and applying three distinct methods. The first approach utilizes the PN spatial density distribution, while the second and third rely on the Planetary Nebula Luminosity Function (PNLF) and the Fundamental Plane (FP), respectively. The first method yields a distance of 20.0 Mpc, whereas the FP-based approach results in 19.6 Mpc. The most reliable estimate comes from the PNLF method, which determines the distance to be 19.3 Mpc. Consequently, we adopt 19.3 Mpc as the definitive distance to the Fornax cluster.

We introduce **LifeStream**, a system designed to analyze massive datasets from production environments while they continue to operate. By utilizing data streams within their native formats, the platform eliminates the performance bottlenecks typically caused by serialization and deserialization. Furthermore, it offers a high-level query language that allows analysts to express complex analytical tasks effortlessly. Despite these capabilities, the approach maintains exceptional speed; when tested against real-world data, **LifeStream** outperforms hand-tuned numerical libraries by a factor of **1,000** and achieves a **100,000x** performance increase over standard applications.

This study investigates the concept of Bertrand curves within definite spaces, specifically focusing on their behavior in both Minkowski space and Minkowski 3-space. The paper examines the properties of Bertrand curves in Minkowski 3-space, categorizing them according to the causal character of the corresponding principal normal vector. Additionally, it analyzes Bertrand spheres in Minkowski space, deriving the necessary and sufficient conditions for a space of constant curvature to possess such spheres.

Although recent research has highlighted the potential of under-represented loss functions such as KL Divergence, we demonstrate that their adoption in specific scenarios can actually degrade performance relative to more common alternatives. To address this, we introduce a novel, flexible framework for loss function selection that surpasses previous methods by utilizing a more comprehensive set of criteria. We validate our approach through an extensive empirical study on the Cora dataset, evaluating 100 distinct neural models and 100 corresponding loss functions. Our findings reveal that while the optimal choice often depends on the specific model architecture, our framework successfully identifies superior options in the vast majority of cases. Furthermore, we observe that the optimal loss function remains largely consistent across different model choices.

This study examines the impact of boundary feedback on the Navier-Stokes equations within a two-dimensional domain, where the feedback is applied at an oblique angle and relies on state information from the system. We establish the existence of a global attractor for the associated semigroup of processes and determine its fractal dimension. Furthermore, we analyze the stability of trivial solutions and demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the feedback induces a Hopf bifurcation.

This study examines the thermomechanical behavior of polymers undergoing strain-induced crystallization, utilizing the framework of rational thermodynamics. The approach relies on the second and first laws of thermodynamics, alongside the principle of equipresence and the concept of a Helmholtz free energy split additively into crystalline and amorphous components. The transition between these phases is governed by a specific nucleation threshold. By applying a variational method to this separation criterion, we derive the conditions for strain-induced crystallization. Furthermore, we develop a constitutive model for a polymer network that incorporates this split criterion, and finally, we validate the model against experimental data concerning the strain-induced crystallization of natural rubber.

We examine the impact of a non-trivial Fermi surface topology on the magnetic field dependence of the spin susceptibility within a superconductor. By applying a self-consistent two-band Nambu formalism, we calculate the full momentum-space distribution of spin susceptibility. Our findings indicate that in a type-II superconductor, the presence of an electron and a hole band yields a distinct bimodal structure, which contrasts with the unimodal profile observed in a single-band type-I superconductor. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this bimodal behavior persists even in a type-II superconductor if the hole band possesses a non-zero Chern number. Finally, we show that the magnitude of the bimodal peaks is governed by the interplay between the Fermi velocities and the interband coupling strength.

The objective is to maximize the quantity of situations in which the agent can apply what it has learned from that feedback. Conventional differential detection for Continuous Phase Modulation (CPM) signals suffers from a relatively high error rate, prompting the need for more effective methods. This study introduces a subcarrier-assisted differential detection scheme that achieves a minimum phase shift of $2\pi/L$, offering an error performance improvement of approximately 10 dB compared to traditional detectors. In this approach, a subcarrier is integrated into the received signal by mixing it with the transmission frequency, $f_t$, to generate a new frequency, $f_t \pm f_s$. The receiver demodulates this modified signal using standard differential detection. The selection of the subcarrier frequency, $f_s$, is critical; specifically, choosing $f_s = 1/L$ ensures the minimum $2\pi/L$ phase transition. The validity of this method is substantiated through both theoretical analysis and simulation results.

We examine the likelihood of generating an electromagnetic counterpart in mergers between two objects with radii $R_1$ and $R_2$ (where $R_1 \ge R_2$), specifically when object 1 is a black hole and object 2 is either a neutron star or a white dwarf. Our analysis indicates that the probability of producing a detectable electromagnetic signal is significantly higher when the neutron star or white dwarf is compact, occurring when the radius ratio $R_1/R_2$ is approximately 1.5 or less. This finding holds true regardless of the black hole's mass or the binary system's eccentricity. These results are particularly relevant for the upcoming era of multi-messenger astronomy, as they will guide the interpretation of observations from facilities such as LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA.

This study examines the applicability of the grand canonical ensemble within systems governed by constant pressure and reveals that validity depends on whether compressibility at constant pressure remains positive. We establish a novel criterion indicating that such systems are effectively equivalent to those held at constant volume when pressure fluctuations are sufficiently suppressed. Additionally, we propose a method to determine the necessary threshold for limiting these fluctuations.

We propose a novel, unified framework that jointly handles raindrop generation and removal. Although these processes appear contradictory, our method treats them as complementary by utilizing a generated rainy image as an intermediate stage. The system consists of two components: a U-Net-based generator that creates rain on a clear image using latent features, and a removal network that takes both the original clear image and the synthetic rainy version as inputs to produce a rain-free output. By training both networks end-to-end with a single loss function, we achieve a unified solution. Experimental results indicate that this method outperforms existing state-of-the-art rain removal algorithms.

We introduce a new approach to acquiring human feedback for reward learning by batching preference comparisons. In this framework, the agent submits groups of $k$-tuples of state-action pairs to the annotator, who ranks them according to the resulting distribution. We demonstrate that the agent can learn a reward function consistent with the provided preferences using significantly fewer samples than traditional methods, which evaluate comparisons one at a time. Our method achieves this by grouping comparisons into batches of size $k$, allowing the agent to learn from the joint outcomes of multiple simultaneous choices. We provide theoretical bounds for this batched active learning strategy and show that it requires far fewer batches compared to the sequential approach. Additionally, we present an efficient algorithm for optimizing the reward function from this batched feedback. Empirical results indicate that this method learns a reward function matching human preferences with a substantial reduction in sample requirements.

This paper investigates the concept of model companionship within set theory, treating it as a first-order theory in variables of any finite arity. It demonstrates that the presence of a model companion is entirely determined by the specific signature in which the underlying set-theoretic axioms are formulated. Additionally, the study examines the model companion of ZFC when expressed in a language augmented with a second-order class predicate.

This study examines the Branson-Paneitz problem defined in $\mathbb{R}^n$ subject to non-standard, inhomogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. We establish the existence of at least one nontrivial critical point for the associated energy functional by applying linking theorem methods. Furthermore, under specific additional hypotheses, we demonstrate the presence of at least two distinct critical points.

This study examines the consumption trends of 14 psychoactive drugs in the United States from 1990 to 2017, utilizing data from the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. By applying a Gaussian Process regression model to analyze consumption patterns across different demographics, we identified significant positive correlations between alcohol, tobacco, and cannabis use. Conversely, consumption of these three substances showed negative correlations with that of amphetamines, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, cocaine, heroin, inhalants, and opioids. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that consumption trends for amphetamines, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, cocaine, heroin, inhalants, and opioids are strongly interlinked, whereas alcohol, tobacco, and cannabis follow distinct trajectories largely independent of the others. These findings indicate that the US drug consumption landscape can be segmented into two primary clusters: one comprising amphetamines, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, cocaine, heroin, inhalants, and opioids, and another consisting of alcohol, tobacco, and cannabis.

We introduce the If-ThenCorpus, a dataset comprising 1,00,000 if-then rules derived from 36,000 unique conditional relationship categories. These data were generated using a hierarchical model of these relationship types trained via a neural approach. Models utilizing these conditional relationships demonstrate performance that surpasses state-of-the-art methods on several natural language inference benchmarks. Furthermore, we discovered that explicitly incorporating the hierarchical architecture of these relationship types yields additional improvements, with our experiments indicating that training on the hierarchical framework of these relationship types provides a significant boost in performance compared to flat models, highlighting the utility of this structured approach in advancing NLI tasks.

We introduce a new implementation of the HHL algorithm variant, designed specifically for current Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) hardware. This approach, termed NISQ-HHL, enhances the standard method by incorporating a modified Cholesky decomposition to decompose the coefficient matrix into sparse triangular components. This decomposition allows the algorithm to transform the original linear system into a sequence of simpler subsystems, each requiring a smaller condition number for the quantum subroutines. By reducing the condition number input to the quantum part of the process, NISQ-HHL enables the use of shorter Toffoli gate sequences and shorter evolution times within the $U(\theta)$ operator, which are critical for mitigating noise on current devices. Our experimental results demonstrate that this method successfully solves a $4\times4$ linear system using a 4-qubit IBM quantum processor.

This study introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism (BiAM) designed to strengthen the interaction between speech embeddings and linguistic data within end-to-end automatic speech recognition systems. In this framework, the attention weights are generated by a bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) network trained on linguistic information, with these weights subsequently applied to align acoustic representations. Experiments conducted on the Librispeech test-clean dataset using a convolutional recurrent neural network (CRNN) with bidirectional GRU acoustic units demonstrate a 2.0% relative improvement in Word Error Rate compared to unidirectional attention, yielding an absolute reduction of 0.9%. Notably, these performance gains were achieved without any additional model parameters or training time.

This note examines the dimensional distinctions in the study of stationary shapes under a conformally modified curvature operator. We analyze these shapes in both two and three dimensions, with the special properties observed in lower dimensions serving as the foundation for defining the concept of "dimension-independent" stationary shapes.

Consider a sequence $k_n/n \to \rho \in (0,1)$ and define the random vector $X_n = (X_n^{(1)}, \dots, X_n^{(k_n)})$, representing the locations of the first $k_n$ cars in a circular "d\'ıııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııııı

We report on the critical current of superconducting nanowires, which are connected in series with resistors, and how this current varies with applied voltage. Our findings reveal that the critical current is highly sensitive to voltage, exhibiting a sharp transition from a linear increase to a linear decrease as voltage rises. This behavior allows the critical current to switch linearly with voltage over a range defined by two critical voltages. By manipulating these voltages through the addition of parallel resistors, we can control the switching point of the critical current's voltage dependence. This phenomenon is explained by a model that attributes the behavior to the interplay between the critical current and the resistance of the normal state.

We present high-resolution near-infrared spectra of the atmosphere of GJ 229B, an intermediate object situated between planets and stars, obtained using the CRIRES+ instrument on the Very Large Telescope. Our spectral analysis yields a mass of $2.81 \pm 0.04 \times 10^{27}$ kg, a radius of $7.04 \pm 0.04 \times 10^7$ m, and an effective temperature of $415 \pm 10$ K. Additionally, we determined the surface gravity to be $12.5 \pm 0.5$ log $g$ cm s$^{-2}$, the rotation period to be $4.8 \pm 0.1$ days, and the projected rotational velocity to be $1.8 \pm 0.1$ km s$^{-1}$. Our findings indicate that the object's rotation is slower than expected for a body of its size and mass, suggesting it has undergone significant angular momentum loss. Furthermore, our measurements of the radius and surface gravity imply the presence of a substantial H/He envelope, with a radius of $2.8 \pm 0.1$ Earth radii and a mass of $4.8 \pm 0.1$ Earth masses. These results offer valuable insights into the formation mechanisms of intermediate bodies occupying the transitional zone between planets and stars.

We derive an exact solution for the initial parton distribution function of a plasma composed of non-interacting quarks and gluons under a sudden, instantaneous expansion from a highly anisotropic state into a perfectly isotropic one. This solution is formulated using the initial distribution in a strongly anisotropic regime, which is constrained by initial temperature and the initial parton density. By employing the AdS/CFT correspondence, we have determined the corresponding strong-coupling limit where quark interactions dominate. At strong coupling, the system exhibits hydrodynamic behavior characterized by a large shear viscosity to entropy density ratio ($\eta/s = 1/2\pi$), causing partons to remain trapped within the medium. Consequently, the strong-coupling parton distribution depends on the coupling parameter $x$ (defined in the introduction), temperature $T$, and the momentum component $p_\perp$. In contrast, in the weak-coupling limit where interactions are negligible, the distribution simplifies to a function of the product $x p_\perp$ and temperature $T$ alone.

This work introduces a new approach to generating videos from unseen camera angles by leveraging the advantages of both implicit and explicit representations. The proposed method employs a dual representation consisting of an explicit Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) alongside an implicit latent code that characterizes views from latent codes. By training this system to predict latent codes for new viewpoints, the method enables efficient rendering of novel views. Experiments indicate that this technique achieves state-of-the-art performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

This study introduces a method for constructing a high-efficiency, two-mode beam splitter for higher-order photonic states using a single, symmetrically tapered nanofiber. By leveraging the strong coupling between a tapered nanofiber and the fundamental modes of two distinct optical fibers, we achieve the splitting of higher-order modes carried by an input fiber. Our theoretical framework demonstrates that this design offers a flexible approach to creating higher-order beam splitters, with tunable characteristics determined by the coupling parameters of the two output fibers.

We propose a novel theoretical framework for the quark model that successfully accounts for the resonance mass spectra of both mesons and baryons. Within this approach, the relativistic two-body system is treated as a single particle moving in a three-dimensional space defined by the center-of-mass coordinates, linear momentum, and an internal variable representing the inter-particle distance. This internal variable is governed by a specific potential function. The resulting mass spectra are derived from a Schrödinger equation formulated in terms of these three dimensions. Our analysis of low-lying meson and baryon spectra reveals that the required potential takes a linear form, consistent with the concept of quark confinement. Furthermore, this model naturally incorporates spin-dependent interactions, including spin-orbit coupling and spin-spin interactions, which are crucial for accurately describing the observed spectral patterns.

This study introduces a straightforward yet effective model for aerosol transmission that accounts for the spatial distribution of particles surrounding an infected person. We contrast this approach with fully well-mixed models and demonstrate that it yields superior predictions of aerosol concentration compared to well-mixed counterparts, particularly in scenarios involving larger particles and higher ventilation rates. Furthermore, we show that this new framework offers more accurate estimates of infection risk than well-mixed models, without requiring the computational complexity of advanced three-dimensional simulations.

This work examines quantum vacuum diffraction and birefringence for X-ray photons traversing the interface between two distinct, uniform electromagnetic fields. We demonstrate that by varying the propagation direction within the field, the degree of diffraction and birefringence can be controlled. Furthermore, we prove that the X-ray vacuum birefringence effect is reciprocal, meaning the photons' polarization state remains unchanged after propagating through the field in one direction and then the opposite direction.

This study introduces an algorithm designed to produce fully transitive polyhedra with specific vertex-, edge-, and face-transitivity properties. The method generates these structures by connecting two given faces through a sequence of shared ridges (edges adjacent to two faces). We demonstrate that this approach yields infinite families of such polyhedra in three-dimensional Euclidean space ($\mathbb{R}^3$), which are realized as geodesic surfaces embedded within that space.

We introduce the concept of encryption that is uncloneable, which ensures that an adversary cannot create two functional decryptions from a single ciphertext. This framework serves as an encryption scheme for functions that cannot be copied and strengthens prior results by offering resilience against passive attackers. Specifically, we present an Uncloneable Encryption (UE) system for functions that resist learning from examples (unlearnable functions) within the model where the adversary has no access to an encryption oracle. This capability implies a stronger form of protection for unlearnable functions than existing copy-secure schemes for such functions, which currently rely on the ability to query an oracle that learns examples. Our construction leverates the existence of indistinguishability obfuscation and encryption schemes secure against selective decryption. Additionally, we propose a concrete instantiation of UE for the specific class of point functions, conditioned on the existence of witness encryption secure for NP relations and code-based obfuscation.

This study introduces a methodology for transforming channels codes into authentication mechanisms, ensuring both integrity and source authentication while maintaining a low error probability. The proposed approach treats the authenticator as a meta-code constructed from an original channel code and a small auxiliary code with a negligible asymptotic rate. By leveraging the inherent error-correction capabilities of the base channel code, the system achieves robustness against errors and authenticates the source without compromising transmission efficiency. Furthermore, the work establishes conditions guaranteeing the optimality of this construction regarding the achievable coding rate and demonstrates its validity for a broad spectrum of authentication protocols.

Using density functional theory, we investigate plasmon behavior in twisted bilayer MoS$_2$ across various lattice relaxations and doping concentrations. Our findings reveal that both lattice relaxation and doping levels significantly influence plasmon energies and their dispersion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these effects are highly sensitive to the twist angle, with the most pronounced changes occurring near the "magic" angle.

This paper examines several properties regarding almost conformal Ricci solitons, specifically addressing the conditions under which an almost conformal Ricci soliton qualifies as an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton, as well as the conditions for an almost conformal Ricci soliton to be reparameterized as a gradient type. Furthermore, the study investigates almost conformal Ricci solitons that are conformal with a constant rate of change, demonstrating that such a soliton can always be reparameterized to become a gradient almost conformal Ricci soliton.

The interaction between magnetospheres and stellar winds is a prevalent natural occurrence across the cosmos, ranging from solar flares and auroras to the potential habitability of exoplanets. While the fundamental physics governing these interactions are well-understood, the complex morphology of magnetospheres formed by such encounters remains poorly characterized. This paper presents a novel, three-dimensional, time-dependent numerical model designed to investigate the formation of both stellar and planetary magnetospheres under varying wind and magnetic field conditions. Our framework employs a hybrid approach, utilizing particle-in-cell methods for the kinetic plasma surrounding a dipolar planet and a magnetohydrodynamic model for the magnetized stellar wind. We apply this model to analyze the magnetospheres of Jupiter and an active K-dwarf star, revealing that the complex structures observed in Jupiter's system are also present on a much smaller scale in the K-dwarf case. Furthermore, our results indicate that magnetospheres are highly dynamic, with significant changes occurring on timescales of minutes to hours.

We have examined the electrical resistivity and Hall effect in Co/Bi multilayers across a broad spectrum of Bi layer thicknesses. Our findings indicate that Bismuth layers serve as a critical tool for manipulating the scattering mechanisms governing the Hall effect in Cobalt. Specifically, as the Bismuth thickness increases, the transition from an extrinsic skew scattering regime to an intrinsic carrier-contraction regime occurs at a significantly lower resistivity threshold compared to pure Cobalt films. This shift is attributed to the substantial modification of Cobalt's electronic structure by the adjacent Bismuth layers.

This study examines numerical solutions to the Schrödinger equation in N dimensions, where the potential includes a fractional parameter $0 < \alpha < 2$. We introduce a numerical scheme utilizing the Split Operator method combined with a spectral approach. The validity of this scheme is confirmed through comparisons with established analytical solutions and other numerical methods. Furthermore, we utilize this scheme to investigate the potential's influence on wave packet dynamics, specifically analyzing how variations in N and $\alpha$ affect tunneling dynamics and spreading rates.

We introduce a novel technique for enforcing a bounded neural network's Lipschitz constant by integrating a specific constraint into the loss function. This approach employs gradient descent to minimize total loss, which combines a standard component with a new term designed to enforce the constant. Our analysis reveals that the network's performance is sensitive to the choice of $p$ in this new term; specifically, using $p=2$ yields superior outcomes compared to other values. We substantiate these findings with both theoretical arguments and experimental results.

Current sequential models rely on local heuristics to capture the hierarchical organization of sentences by attending to nearby words, yet they lack an explicit representation of such hierarchy. This study introduces Hierarchical Recurrent Attention (HRA), a sequential framework that combines hierarchical structure with local attention mechanisms. HRA constructs a contextually appropriate tree structure through a bottom-up process, where nodes are determined by attending to their immediate children. Additionally, HRA incorporates a top-down refinement process that updates node contexts by attending to their parents. Experiments on sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, and semantic role labeling demonstrate that HRA achieves state-of-the-art results using both pre-trained and randomly initialized embeddings.

The extreme eccentricity of the orbit of HD 80606b drives dramatic variations in the irradiation received by the planet, causing its effective temperature to shift from 1060 K at apastron to 1950 K at periastron. This study presents new, high-resolution near-infrared spectra captured at multiple orbital phases, which were analyzed using both line-mapping and equilibrium temperature models. The observed spectral changes are well-explained by the migration of the line-of-sight terminator across the planetary surface. Furthermore, the data indicate that the global heat redistribution is inefficient, with an estimated efficiency of only 10%–20%.

Gamified rehabilitation exercises can boost user engagement and motivation, yet the design of such games often requires careful tuning of interaction parameters to balance engagement with therapeutic efficacy. This study introduces a method to automatically identify these parameters by analyzing player data, utilizing a fitness-focused gamified game as a case study. The proposed approach employs a multi-objective optimization algorithm to automatically search for optimal settings. Results indicate that this method successfully identifies parameters that enhance both engagement and rehabilitation outcomes, offering a practical solution to improve future game designs.

We examine the relationship between brittle fracture energies in geometrically nonlinear elasticity and linearised elasticity. Our approach involves deriving a $\Gamma$-convergence result for a family of constrained minimisation problems. We establish that the constrained minimisers of the brittle fracture energy, when viewed under the framework of linearised elasticity, are precisely those satisfying the non-linearised elasticity equations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the corresponding relaxed constrained brittle fracture energies are equivalent to those derived by Friesecke and Müller (2001).

This study introduces the first LHC search for vector leptoquarks (LQs) utilizing the NLO+PS approach. We examine the sensitivity of the ATLAS detector to single-productions of LQs that decay into a muon and a neutrino, focusing on the signature of a muon plus missing transverse momentum. We compare results using the standard NLO approach against the NLO+PS method, highlighting that the latter significantly improves signal modeling by enhancing the accuracy of single LQ kinematics and the overall missing transverse momentum distribution. Consequently, the NLO+PS framework yields a more favorable signal-to-background ratio and a more optimal selection efficiency.

This study introduces a novel, fully convolutional deep neural network (DNN) designed to enhance low-dose Positron Emission Tomography (PET) images by integrating structural information from corresponding Magnetic Resonance (MRI) scans. The proposed architecture consists of two parallel branches: the first processes the low-dose PET image, while the second handles the MRI data. These branches are followed by multiple convolutional layers and a skip-connection mechanism that merges the refined low-dose PET features with the corresponding MRI-derived structural features. The integrated combined features are then utilized to reconstruct a high-quality enhanced low-dose PET image. Experimental evaluations indicate that this approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in both quantitative metrics and visual assessments.

This study examines user attitudes toward news personalization and privacy, utilizing a two-stage approach. The first phase involved a survey of 1,000 U.S. participants regarding their news consumption habits, their views on personalized recommendations, and their privacy concerns. The second phase employed a discrete choice experiment (DCE) with a subset of 300 respondents to assess their trade-offs between personalization and privacy. The DCE presented respondents with various news platform profiles differing in personalization levels, privacy risk levels, and pricing, alongside demographic data. The study reveals that while the majority of respondents value news personalization, they simultaneously express significant worries about privacy. Furthermore, the analysis indicates that age is a critical factor influencing these attitudes.

Although recent studies indicate that contextualized embeddings significantly enhance various natural language processing tasks, their ability to improve neural coreference resolution remains unclear. This study investigates the impact of these embeddings on a neural coreference model built upon the principles of centering theory. We evaluate the model using the CoNLL-2012 dataset, comparing the performance of various embedding types against a baseline of character-level inputs. Results show that the model achieves a 0.74 F1 score with the COREE dataset, improving by 0.01 over the baseline. Furthermore, analysis reveals that the model's ability to predict antecedents and the strength of preference scores are both positively influenced by the quality of the embeddings. Finally, we examine the model's behavior when predicting antecedents versus non-antecedents, specifically analyzing the associated preference scores.

This work examines parameterized algorithmic approaches for directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) utilizing treewidth. We introduce the concept of DAG-treewidth, a DAG-specific variant of treewidth that effectively parameterizes several algorithms addressing problems such as the longest path, k-vertex disjoint paths, and the longest cycle. Furthermore, we present a new parameterized algorithm for the longest cycle problem in general graphs with running time of $2^{\text{DAG-treewidth} \cdot \text{treewidth}} \cdot n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$. This result improves upon the previous best-known complexity of $2^{\text{treewidth}^2} \cdot n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$ by a factor of $\text{treewidth}$ in the exponent.

Utilizing optimization techniques to configure system settings can yield enhanced performance, reduced costs, and greater efficiency. Furthermore, this approach often clarifies the relationship between input parameters and system behavior, thereby improving human comprehension. In this paper, we apply such optimization strategies to configure the S3 bucket policy for a machine learning training pipeline on AWS. Our configuration achieves a 20% reduction in training latency while simultaneously decreasing S3 costs by 30%, all within a 10-hour period.

We investigate the evolution of operators within non-interacting quantum systems governed by Hamiltonians possessing specific symmetries. By decomposing operators into irreducible components of the symmetry group, we demonstrate that operator growth decomposes into independent contributions from each component. We further establish that key metrics of growth—Krylov complexity and the out-of-time-order correlator (OTOC)—can be significantly simplified by utilizing these symmetry-based components. Our analysis focuses on systems with translation symmetry, employing both momentum space (where symmetries simplify calculations due to their inherent nature) and real-space representations (where the advantage is less obvious). We find that Krylov complexity achieves its simplest form when computed via symmetry-adapted components in momentum space. Additionally, we examine the dynamics of the symmetry-resolved OTOC, highlighting how its behavior depends on the growth rates of individual components and their mutual interference patterns.

This study introduces a machine learning framework designed to enhance the accuracy of geospatial distance estimation between WiFi location signatures. By accurately forecasting this distance, we aim to improve the overall performance of WiFi-based localization systems. Our method utilizes a Random Forest regressor to model the distance between fingerprints, leveraging diverse environmental features. We specifically examine the impact of estimating distance on locating accuracy within a three-cell framework, where the geospatial distance determines the weight distribution across neighboring cells. Evaluation using the MIT Indoor dataset demonstrates that our approach yields a mean estimated geospatial distance of 19.6 meters, with a standard deviation of 11.1 meters. Consequently, this model achieves a localization accuracy of 91.3%.

The Kardashev scale categorizes civilizations by their energy utilization, with Type II entities harnessing the full solar output of their star. While Type II structures like Dyson spheres have long been theoretical constructs, recent research suggests that a Type II civilization might instead employ a swarm of smaller, mobile collectors. This study investigates the potential luminosity of such a swarm when positioned in a highly elliptical orbit around a star, revealing that orbital dynamics can amplify total emitted light by a factor of 1.5 to 2 compared to a circular path. Furthermore, the study explores the impact of varying collector distances on the system's brightness, demonstrating that an optimal configuration exists which boosts luminosity by approximately 1.1 times beyond a circular orbit. These findings offer significant implications for the design of future space-based solar energy systems and the methods used to identify them.

This paper introduces a Peer-to-Peer (P2P) framework designed to track Service Level Agreement (SLA) breaches in network performance. In this system, each SLA provider is assigned a set of dedicated peers responsible for monitoring the SLA's performance. To ensure accurate SLA assessment, the proposed approach employs a novel, resilient estimation technique for network performance that remains robust against malicious or faulty P2N nodes. Furthermore, the study presents a new algorithm for selecting an optimal subset of peers to track each SLA, optimizing the system based on specific SLA requirements and network conditions. Simulation results indicate that this method effectively detects SLA violations while maintaining low computational and communication overhead.

In a multi-pass energy recovery linac (ERL), the selection of filling patterns critically determines how beams interact with radio-frequency fields and sets the minimum threshold current. This study examines various filling patterns within a two-bunch-mode ERL configuration, utilizing full six-dimensional macro-particle simulations to evaluate their impact on beam-rf interactions and threshold currents. Our findings indicate that filling patterns significantly influence these outcomes; specifically, a pattern that distributes particles uniformly across both bunches yields the lowest threshold current. Conversely, a pattern that concentrates particles into a single bunch results in the highest beam loss, reaching approximately 10% higher than the baseline single-bunch operation.

This study presents a measurement of the total neutron cross section for scintillator targets across the energy range from 98 to 688 MeV, utilizing the Mini-JPARC external neutron beam. Neutron fluxes were determined via the hadron flux and the inclusive single-pion production cross sections, which were derived from the observed final states. The resulting cross sections for neutron scintillator annihilation are presented as an average of three distinct energy intervals: [98, 160] MeV, [160, 350] MeV, and [350, 688] MeV. We conducted experiments to measure the increase in sticking forces for super-dry granular samples across a range of temperatures from 200 to 1,000 K. Our findings indicate that sticking forces increase by approximately one order of magnitude between 200 and 400 K, with a more pronounced rise observed at higher temperatures. We attribute this increase to the formation of hydrogen bonds between particles, which becomes more significant as temperature rises. Based on these results, we propose that planetesimal formation likely occurred within a temperature range of 200–400 K, where sticking forces are substantially higher than in current protoplanetary disc conditions.

Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) serves as a dimensionality reduction technique well-suited for high-dimensional, low-sample scenarios, offering the advantages of both LDA and its locality-aware counterpart, NLDA. This study evaluates the performance of LFDA and its variants using the `leda` R package, which handles computations and generates corresponding visualizations. The analysis was conducted on three datasets: the Wine dataset, the Ion Chromatography dataset, and the Leukemia dataset. Results indicate that LFDA and its variants effectively preserve local data structures while maintaining class separability.

Imitation learning enables robots to acquire skills from demonstrations, yet most existing methods focus on unconstrained tasks and struggle to manage complex, nonlinear safety constraints. Constrained Imitation Learning (CIL) addresses this gap by enabling robots to master skills from human instructors while adhering to safety-critical constraints. A primary hurdle in CIL is ensuring that a demonstration's implicit knowledge of these constraints is successfully transferred to the robot. To this end, we introduce a novel approach that leverages the redundancy of a robot's null-space to learn safe skills from noisy, corrupted demonstrations. Our method allows for the inclusion of arbitrary nonlinear safety constraints directly within the objective function, utilizing a weighted least-squares framework. By applying a null-space projection to the demonstration data, our approach ensures that the learned policy strictly satisfies all constraints while remaining close to the original behavior. We validate our method through simulations and physical experiments on a seven-degree-of-freedom arm, demonstrating its ability to accurately reproduce noisy demonstrations even when navigating highly constrained workspaces.

We present the computation of the two-gluon color-even scalar vacuum (CEV) amplitudes for six and seven gluons within QCD. These results are derived by applying the Bern-Dixon-Smirnov (BDS) ansatz to the known amplitudes of six-gluon scalar amplitudes in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory. Our analysis indicates that the two-gluon CEV amplitude for six gluons aligns perfectly with the ansatz at $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s^4)$, while for six-gluon cases at $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s^5)$, it matches the ansatz for all but one specific coefficient. Furthermore, we have determined the two-gluon CEV amplitude for six-gluon cases at $\mathcal{O}(\alpha_s^5)$ at leading order in the strong coupling constant. We examine the interplay among spin-orbit coupling, superconductivity, and a periodic potential within a minimal two-band model. By utilizing a Bogoliubov-de Gennes framework, we demonstrate that spin-orbit coupling can induce a topological transition in the superconducting state, generating non-zero topological invariants. Furthermore, we show that introducing band hybridization allows for the manipulation of these topological characteristics, specifically enabling the emergence of gapless Majorana surface states.

We have measured the specific heat of $\text{YBa}_2\text{Cu}_3\text{O}_{6.95}$ single crystals with varying thicknesses to determine the specific heat jump across the superconducting transition within the vortex lattice phase. Our findings indicate that vortex lattice melting occurs at a temperature significantly lower than the specific heat jump associated with the superconducting transition itself. Furthermore, the magnitude of this specific heat jump aligns well with theoretical predictions for $d$-wave superconductivity near van Hove singularities. These outcomes support the conclusion that vortex lattice melting corresponds to a first-order transition, whereas the primary specific heat jump arises from a second-order transition.

This study examines the equilibrium configurations and mechanical properties of polymer brushes anchored to curved substrates. By applying the self-consistent field theory framework, we analyze polymers grafted onto both concave and convex surfaces with varying curvatures. Our findings indicate that the free energy associated with stretching increases as surface curvature rises. Consequently, both the lateral and longitudinal elastic moduli of the brush layer are found to decrease with increasing curvature. Additionally, we explore the equilibrium states of a curved substrate subjected to lateral tension, observing that tension induces a retraction of the brush away from the surface. In the case of a concave interface, this tension triggers a phase transition characterized by the emergence of a polymer-depleted region near the center of curvature.

We examine the truncated graph metric dimension, defined as the smallest size of a set $F \subset V(G)$ that uniquely identifies every vertex $v \in V(G)$ based on its distances to nodes in $F$, where these distances are capped at a threshold $\tau \ge 1$. We demonstrate that for any fixed graph $G$ and $\tau$, this dimension is bounded by a function dependent solely on $\tau$ and the standard metric dimension of $G$. Furthermore, we analyze specific families of graphs, including trees, grids, and Cayley graphs, to determine how the truncated metric dimension varies with $\tau$. Finally, we address the computational complexity of locating an identifying set for this metric under the given truncation.

Active galactic nuclei (AGN) display variability across numerous timescales, yet reconstructing their intrinsic variability from incomplete, irregularly sampled data remains challenging. This study introduces a novel method utilizing Gaussian processes (GPs) to reconstruct the intrinsic variability of AGN light curves. We applied this technique to the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) AGN catalog, which comprises 1,000 light curves with irregular sampling spanning 10 to 20 years. Our approach effectively recovers variability timescales ranging from 100 days to 10 years and reveals that most AGN exhibit timescales between 1 and 10 years. Additionally, we demonstrate that the method successfully reconstructs variability even in light curves with gaps of up to 100 days.

We introduce a broad class of valuation structures grounded in bipartite matchings and directed graphs, encompassing additively separable, gross substitutes, and unit demand valuations. We propose two novel randomized mechanisms tailored to these valuations, both achieving an $O(\log^2 n)$ approximation for social welfare. Notably, the first mechanism is truthful in expectation, while the second is fully truthful; furthermore, we establish a matching lower bound of $\Omega(\log n)$ for the latter.

Binary asteroids are frequently identified as candidates through wide-field surveys by analyzing the Point Spread Function (PSF) of stellar point sources. However, the effectiveness of this method relies on the assumption that stellar PSFs remain constant across the field of view, an assumption often violated in large telescopes. This study introduces a new technique for PSF analysis that does not require such uniformity. The approach involves fitting a PSF model to a single star and then comparing the residual differences between the model and the observed data. We demonstrate that this method can detect binary asteroids with a signal-to-noise ratio of at least 3, provided the primary component has a signal-to-noise ratio exceeding 10. Additionally, we show that this approach can estimate the magnitude of PSF variations across the field, which is valuable for optimizing the selection of target stars.

This study presents a new, straightforward, and efficient method for estimating network peer effects, addressing both linear and non-linear specifications. The proposed approach utilizes a simple instrumental variable framework, where the instrument is derived from a network matrix constructed from exogenous variables. We validate the framework through Monte Carlo simulations and apply it to two instances of network interdependence in the empirical section: first, analyzing how firms' R&D productivity relies on the R&D activity of their network partners, and second, examining how non-cognitive skills are influenced by the behaviors of peers within a school's social network.

This study introduces novel integral representations and associated chain rule formulas for variable-order fractional operators. Specifically, three distinct types of chain rule formulas are established: one addressing single composition, another for double composition, and a third for multiply composed operators. Furthermore, the work defines variable-order fractional integration by parts, complemented by several related formulas.

This study examines the performance of an optimal Bayesian detector, which is computationally intractable, for a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) system employing a binary phase-shift keying (BPSK) scheme. This specific detector utilizes prior information regarding the probability of bit errors. Our analysis demonstrates that this detector achieves a significantly lower error rate compared to other methods, including the optimal maximum-likelihood (ML) detector, the approximate Bayesian detector, and various linear and non-linear equalizers. Although the error rate for the intractable optimal Bayesian detector is substantially lower, the corresponding likelihood function cannot be computed efficiently. Consequently, we propose a Monte Carlo integration-based approximation to enable the practical implementation of this optimal detector. Simulation results indicate that this proposed approach yields an error rate nearly identical to that of the theoretical optimal detector.

BPT diagrams serve as a fundamental tool for analyzing galaxy spectra, enabling the classification of ionization sources and the measurement of physical properties such as stellar masses and star formation rates. This study presents a Bayesian framework for estimating these parameters using BPT diagram data, specifically designed to handle the complex, multi-modal nature of BPT distributions. We introduce a novel mixture model that combines a Gaussian component with a non-parametric kernel density estimator to capture both the primary and minor modes within these distributions. By applying this approach to the SDSS-IV extended BPT dataset, we demonstrate that the method successfully recovers the underlying distributions of galaxy properties, including star formation rates and stellar masses, while also providing a flexible means to define BPT regions.

The breakup of Gondwana was driven by the opening of the South Atlantic Ocean, a process that involved significant changes in the orientation and speed of extensional forces. This study utilizes a geodynamic model to examine how these variations influenced the formation of Gondwana's coastal geological structures. The model incorporates a Gondwana-style lithosphere with a subducted African margin and a passive South American margin, situated within a domain featuring a thickened cratonic keel and a thin, attenuated continental margin. Our results indicate that the shift in extension direction and the increase in breakup velocity triggered the development of a dense, mantle-derived mafic underplating structure along the eastern Brazilian margin. This underplating is responsible for generating the distinct marginal geological features observed in the region today.

We introduce a novel unsupervised pre-training framework designed to enhance segmentation capabilities by leveraging the inherent structure of point clouds. This approach relies on two core innovations: first, the Self-Alignment Principle, which posits that points within a local neighborhood should exhibit similar features; and second, the Self-Completion Principle, which suggests that a complete local neighborhood can be reconstructed from partial observations. Guided by these concepts, we propose a new method for generating self-supervised neighborhood labels. Additionally, we develop a dual-stream network architecture that incorporates both a neighborhood completion task and a self-label alignment task to achieve robust pre-training. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets confirm that this method yields significant improvements over state-of-the-art unsupervised segmentation techniques.

We introduce a novel framework for solving cooperative games by integrating a theory-of-mind approach that incorporates an explicit model of another agent's goals. In this setting, a learner interacts within a partially observable Markov decision process with a teacher, aiming to achieve a shared objective through trial-and-error. The learner constructs a theory-of-mind representation of the teacher, specifically modeling their goal structure, to guide its actions. We evaluate this method on two benchmark tasks: a simplified collaborative game and the multi-agent pathfinding problem found in the Maze2 environment from the Meta-World suite. Results indicate that this theory-of-mind strategy significantly outperforms baseline approaches in both tasks, achieving higher goal attainment rates and demonstrating greater sample efficiency.

Words often experience semantic shifts over time, a phenomenon that poses significant challenges for Natural Language Processing (NLP). While large pre-trained language models (LMs) have proven effective at capturing linguistic nuances, their static nature prevents them from adapting to these temporal changes. To address this, we propose a method that leverages fine-tuning to discover new terminology and vocabulary within specific timeframes. By training an LM on a corpus from a specific era, we can identify emerging words and their definitions, enabling the creation of time-sensitive language models. This approach allows us to detect words that undergo semantic drift, such as "cool," and uncover words with entirely novel meanings, like "tweet."

We introduce novel functions designed to connect the transverse dynamics of partons within hadrons to observable hadronic processes. These functions are constructed to maintain gauge invariance and satisfy specific sum rules, with evolution equations derived that are analogous to the DGLAP formalism. Although our framework encompasses and extends previous ideas, it offers distinct advantages: it is formulated as a gauge-invariant set, and its connection to physical observables is more direct.

The folding mechanisms of knotted proteins are significantly more intricate than those of unknotted proteins, largely due to the rarity of knotted topologies in nature. While the folding routes of deeply knotted proteins have been extensively documented, the pathways for shallow knotted proteins remain poorly understood. This study utilizes molecular dynamics simulations to contrast the folding trajectories of shallow and deeply knotted proteins, revealing that these pathways diverge markedly. Specifically, the formation of knotted structures in shallow proteins occurs via a single, distinct route, whereas deeply knotted proteins adopt multiple distinct formation mechanisms. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that the folding process for shallow knotted proteins adheres to a three-state model, whereas deeply knotted proteins follow a complex, multi-state trajectory. These findings offer new insights into the fundamental principles governing protein folding.

We investigate Early Dark Energy (EDE) as a potential solution to the Hubble Tension, specifically examining how constraints on the allowed fraction of the universe's energy density in this dark energy component evolve when utilizing different cosmological frameworks. By analyzing likelihood distributions for EDE parameters within three distinct models—the standard $\Lambda$CDM, the standard $\Lambda$CDM with a running spectral index, and the standard $\Lambda$CDM with a running spectral index and primordial gravitational wave amplitude—we determine the permissible ranges for the EDE fraction. Our findings indicate that allowing the primordial gravitational wave amplitude ($f_A$) to vary significantly relaxes these constraints, resulting in EDE fractions that are notably larger than those permitted under the fixed-$f_A$ $\Lambda$CDM scenario. Furthermore, incorporating the running spectral index ($\alpha_s$) also influences the allowed values, with the magnitude of this effect contingent upon the specific cosmological model employed.
