We examine a model where a Nambu-Goldstone boson (the NGb) acquires mass via its interaction with a new strongly coupled sector, specifically through kaon condensation. This framework is analyzed using the linear sigma model, with the new sector's dynamics described by a linearly realized $SU(3)_L \times SU(3)_R$ chiral symmetry. In this model, the NGb emerges as a linear combination of the pions and the singlet $\eta'$ field. We establish that the NGb's mass and its coupling to two NGbs are determined by the symmetry-breaking pattern and the specific structure of the strong sector. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the NGb's self-coupling is directly proportional to the ratio of the strong scale to the NGb's mass, a relationship that can be utilized to constrain the model's parameters. Finally, we calculate the partial decay widths of the NGb into two and three NGbs, as well as its production cross-section in gluon fusion at the LHC.

We introduce DISCO, a framework that creates counterfactual training data to enhance model robustness and generalization. Our method identifies the most influential features driving overconfident, incorrect predictions and generates synthetic inputs that alter these features while maintaining similar output probabilities. Empirical results on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 demonstrate that training with these counterfactuals significantly improves adversarial robustness and out-of-distribution generalization.

This paper establishes equitable neighborhood sum distinguishing colorings for the edges and incident vertices of a circulant graph $Ch(\{2,3\},s)$ using just three colors, whenever $s$ is an odd integer greater than or equal to 5. As a direct outcome, both the equitable sum distinguishing chromatic number and the standard sum distinguishing chromatic number for edge-vertex distinguishing colorings of $Ch(\{2,3\},s)$ are equal to 3 under these specified conditions.

We investigated the temperature-dependent growth of epitaxial graphene on Si(001) substrates, utilizing scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) to examine the resulting surface structures. Our findings reveal that varying growth temperatures induce distinct structural phases: low-temperature synthesis yields a single domain characterized by a 2×1 lattice reconstruction, whereas high-temperature synthesis produces two separate domains—a 2×1 lattice and a 3×2 lattice. Furthermore, we determined that the 3×2 domain consists of two distinct sub-domains, each possessing a unique atomic arrangement. To elucidate the underlying mechanisms, we employed a tight-binding model to calculate the electronic structures of these various lattices. Finally, we analyzed the formation of these domains through the lens of strain energy and electronic energy.

In this study, we derive both upper and lower bounds for the ranks of $\mathbb{Z}_3\mathbb{Z}_9$-linear codes and establish their significance in determining the construction of such structures. By applying these findings, we generate several new $\mathbb{Z}_3\mathbb{Z}_9$-linear codes that achieve optimality within their respective parameters.

This study examines the polymer injection process within a mixing zone, where two immiscible fluids flow between parallel plates under a pressure gradient. The flowing fluids are characterized by Newtonian and non-Newtonian viscosities, with the latter defined by a specific viscosity function. By utilizing a Hele-Shaw approximation, we derive a one-dimensional Hele-Shaw model and solve it to determine the velocity profile and the position of the displacement front. Our analysis reveals that the shape of the viscosity function critically influences the polymer distribution and the overall mixing zone profile. Furthermore, we validate our theoretical findings through direct numerical simulations (DNS) based on the full Navier-Stokes equations.

Annotating multi-label datasets is resource-intensive, as annotators must provide all labels for every single sample. To alleviate this burden, we introduce S2M, a novel annotation method where annotators supply only one label per sample, effectively generating multiple labels through data augmentation. Although this approach significantly reduces costs, it creates a discrepancy between the data used for training (containing multiple labels) and the annotation schema (single label per sample). To bridge this gap, we present a new training framework that trains a multi-label classifier on data generated via S2M. Specifically, we employ a contrastive learning strategy that pulls positive instances sharing the same label closer in the embedding space while pushing negative instances further apart. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing baselines, achieving superior performance with a fraction of the required annotation effort.

This work presents a numerical approach for the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation, utilizing a numerical integration scheme for the fractional derivative that is second-order accurate in time. The proposed method employs a fully discrete, energy-stable, second-order compact difference scheme. This scheme maintains second-order accuracy for both space and time, incorporates an energy norm that is equivalent to the $H^1$ norm, and ensures the solution adheres to the energy-dissipating characteristics of the original equation. Theoretical analysis and numerical simulations confirm the scheme's convergence, stability, and its ability to accurately capture the energy-dissipating behavior of the problem. Notably, the proposed method is applicable to equations where the fractional derivative parameter $\alpha$ equals 1, as well as to the standard integer-order (second) Allen-Cahn equation.

In any category possessing finite products, the concept of a "pointed object" can be defined either as an object equipped with a morphism from the finite product to itself or as an object admitting a projection to it. We demonstrate that these two definitions are equivalent under the condition of weak naturality. Furthermore, we examine the structure of weakly natural transformations between two such pointed objects, showing that they constitute a category that is functorially and universally related to the underlying product of the standard natural transformation sets associated with the pointed objects. Our analysis of this framework is motivated by the study of pointed adjunctions, where we establish that the collection of adjunction pairs compatible with a specific fixed pointed object forms a category. We also introduce the definition of a "pointed monad," which we argue is particularly significant in the context of the "free-forgetful" adjunction arising from algebras over a monad.

We utilize the MAD model to examine GeV gamma-ray observations of the Galactic Center, focusing on the role of electron heating. Our findings indicate that incorporating heating is essential to accurately model the data, with the required GeV flux being highly sensitive to the magnitude of the electron heating rate. Specifically, the heating rate must be approximately 100 times greater than the heating rate associated with protons to account for the observed GeV data. We further explore the implications of this elevated heating rate for the ionized gas within the Galactic Center, concluding that it could resolve the discrepancy between the observed X-ray emission and the predicted X-ray recombination lines.

This study examines the impact of a stochastic time change on the distribution of asset return intervals, specifically analyzing how the first four moments of cross-sectional return data across fixed durations relate to the underlying time interval moment structure. The analysis demonstrates that the resulting empirical distribution of returns can be reconstructed by integrating the true cumulative distribution function against a weighting scheme derived from the time change's moments. This approach allows for the identification of plausible families of return distribution models by fitting the observed data. Furthermore, the methodology is extended to address multivariate scenarios, where the study investigates the implications for the cross-sectional distribution of return vectors.

This study introduces a new approach to detecting cardiac anomalies using only noisy, uncurated audio from wearables. Leveraging deep learning, the method employs an audio classification model trained on a curated subset of heart sounds to identify abnormal sounds within vast collections of imperfect data. To achieve this, we propose a novel self-supervised learning framework that uses a contrastive model to map sounds to latent representations, enabling the system to learn from the inherent structure of the data itself. Wearable sensors have become essential for monitoring daily human activities, yet current activity recognition systems often struggle with accuracy when processing data from diverse users. To address this, researchers have explored Federated Learning (FL) to keep data localized, but applying FL to wearable activity recognition faces unique hurdles. First, the vast variety of activities and the need for extensive training samples make FL training slow and resource-intensive. Second, the diversity in how different users move creates significant challenges for creating a shared global model. To overcome these issues, we introduce FedHealth, a user-centric FL framework that trains models independently for each user and aggregates them afterward. By maintaining separate local models, FedHealth reduces training time and resources while preserving high accuracy. Experiments on the large-scale Smart-2020 dataset demonstrate that FedHealth achieves a 98.1% accuracy rate, outperforming standard FL approaches by 2.3% and centralised methods by 0.4%. Furthermore, it surpasses the performance of the original paper's model by 1.3%, even when using only 10% of the available data.

This study evaluates two optimization approaches—utility-based and multi-objective—for generating Pareto-optimal portfolios. We utilize a synthetic asset class featuring a hierarchical structure of risk factors to create a portfolio optimization problem. Our methodology involves comparing the solutions derived from a traditional utility optimization framework against those obtained via a multi-objective optimization (MOO) method employing the $\epsilon$-constraint technique. The results indicate that the utility optimization approach yields a limited set of solutions, whereas the $\epsilon$-constraint MOO method successfully produces the full spectrum of Pareto-optimal portfolios. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the specific selection of a utility function significantly influences the resulting portfolio outcomes.

We introduce a model of dark energy where the quintessence field couples to heavy states via a Higgs portal, generating an effective potential through coherent oscillations. This framework allows for the reconstruction of cosmic history by coupling to the Higgs field with strength $\lambda_{\chi H}$, which determines the magnitude of the effective potential. Specifically, we examine two scenarios: coupling to the bare Higgs field and coupling to the Higgs field squared. In both cases, we analyze how varying $\lambda_{\chi H}$ influences the dark energy equation of state and the universe's evolutionary trajectory. Our findings indicate that this model can successfully describe a matter-dominated era followed by a dark energy-dominated era, with the transition occurring at a scale of approximately $10^{-3}$ eV. Furthermore, we explore the implications of this model on the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and large-scale structure (LSS), finding that it remains consistent with current observational data.

Recruiting qualified candidates for a role typically involves scheduling interviews with multiple stakeholders, such as peers and decision-makers, and subsequently assembling interview panels. This paper proposes algorithmic methods to streamline both the interview scheduling process and the panel generation. We demonstrate that these approaches are highly effective in real-world scenarios, significantly reducing the manual administrative burden on recruiters.

This study examines the optimal payoff within a class of backward stochastic differential equations featuring a coupled term involving an underlying diffusion, subject to constraints on the coupled component. We establish the existence of an equivalent control problem whose solution yields a strictly positive optimal payoff, which strictly exceeds that of any other non-satisfactory control. Leveraging this control problem, we derive a coupled system of partial differential equations (specifically, a Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs (HJI) equation pair) that the optimal value function and its gradient must satisfy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the unique viscosity solution to this HJI equation system provides the solution to the original optimal control problem.

This study examines the asymmetric leptoquark (LQ) pair production mechanism within the context of the $B$-meson anomaly. We analyze the anomaly's compatibility with LQ models by exploring the parameter space for both vector and scalar LQs, considering scenarios where the LQ couples to left- and right-handed quarks and leptons with varying masses and coupling strengths. Our analysis reveals that the asymmetric LQ mechanism is viable only if the LQ mass remains below approximately 1.4 TeV and the coupling strength exceeds $10^{-2}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the LQ model can simultaneously account for the $B$-anomaly and the observed LHC diphoton excess, provided the LQ mass is less than 1.2 TeV.

Time-dependent gene expression datasets are frequently utilized to identify variables predictive of specific phenotypes. We propose a method that integrates relevance learning with support vector regression (SVR) to create a new approach, termed Support Vector Regression with Learned Relevance (SVRLR). This framework formulates a two-stage optimization problem: the first stage determines the weights assigned to each variable, while the second stage predicts the target value using these weighted variables. By applying this method to time-dependent gene expression data, we can efficiently isolate predictive features. We evaluated SVRLR against state-of-the-art techniques on both simulated and real-world datasets. Results demonstrate that SVRLR successfully identifies predictive variables and yields prediction accuracy comparable to leading existing methods.

We present new observations of the far-infrared fine-structure line emissions at 25.9, 34.9, and 44.9 $\mu$m for the extreme starburst galaxies ESO 320-G3, Mrk 231, and Mrk 273. These data were collected using the Herschel PACS instrument, with the 142 GHz line ($25.9\ \mu$m) also captured via the IRAM 30m radio telescope. In all three galaxies, the line flux ratios indicate the presence of low-density molecular outflows or circumgalactic gas reservoirs. Specifically, the observed ratios in Mrk 231 and Mrk 273 are significantly higher than those predicted by local thermal equilibrium models for typical interstellar conditions. Additionally, the observed 214 GHz to 142 GHz line flux ratios in ESO 320-G3 are consistent with those found in local starburst galaxies, implying that the impact of low-density gas on the 214/142 GHz ratio is negligible. These findings suggest that the 214/142 GHz line flux ratio serves as a more sensitive indicator of low-density gas than the 46.9/25.9 GHz ratio. Consequently, the results support the hypothesis that extreme starburst galaxies possess extended, low-density molecular gas structures.

We examine the recent flavor anomalies observed within the $K$ and $B$ meson sectors, specifically those involving lepton-flavor universality violations and flavor-changing neutral currents with photons. These inconsistencies are effectively encapsulated by a single new physics scale, $\Lambda_{\rm NP} \sim 25$ TeV. We subsequently analyze the implications of these anomalies for the stability of the electroweak scale, demonstrating that within a generic effective field theory framework, the absence of fine-tuning at the 100-level necessitates stabilizing mechanisms operating at or below $\Lambda_{\rm NP}$.

This paper addresses the challenge of identifying the maximum overlap between two metric balls within a Cayley graph defined by the Hamming distance, where the generating set comprises all vectors of a fixed weight $w$. The radius of the first ball is $r_1$, while the second ball's radius $r_2$ is determined by the graph element's distance $d$ from the first ball's center. The paper presents an explicit formula for the largest possible radius $r_2$ as a function of $w$, $r_1$, and $d$. Additionally, the paper derives the complete collection of $d$ values that yield the maximal $r_2$, along with the corresponding sets of generators of maximal weight $W$ for which this maximum is achieved.

We introduce a new method for identifying musical instruments from recordings of piano, guitar, and violin playing, utilizing only the instrument names as supervision. Our approach employs hierarchical prototypical networks, which organize embeddings into a hierarchical structure that mirrors the taxonomic relationships of instruments. We propose a novel loss function that enforces this hierarchical organization by grouping similar items into tight clusters while maintaining distinct separation between dissimilar ones. Experiments indicate that this framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MusiNet dataset. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our model supports flexible inference; it can function as a binary classifier, a three-way instrument recognizer, or any other hierarchical classification scheme appropriate to the task.

We introduce QASPER, a dataset comprising 1,000 questions that require answering from one or multiple medical documents, such as abstracts, full articles, or passages. These queries span various types, including those demanding aggregation, contradiction resolution, and more. To address them, systems must perform tasks like entity and relation extraction, as well as document selection. We offer two versions of each question: an original form and a simplified variant. Our analysis reveals that current state-of-the-art models struggle with these queries, suggesting ample opportunities for improvement. Through an evaluation of leading models, we reveal that existing systems often fail to correctly identify relevant documents or accurately extract answers. To support this resource, we provide a robust scoring system designed to assess questions based on their difficulty.

We introduce a set of approximate analytic formulas for the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and the posterior probability density of pulsar timing array (PTA) signals sourced by stochastic gravitational wave backgrounds (GWBs). These expressions are derived using the Gaussian assumption regarding GWB parameters and the Gaussian assumption regarding the covariance of single-toiled pulsar timing residuals. Our approach accounts for the full complexity of the NANOGrav 15-pc data release 1 (DR1) model, specifically incorporating individual pulsar parameters, the full covariance matrix of timing residuals, and the spectral shape of the GWB. We validate these formulas against the NANOGrav 15-pc DR1 results and find that they are accurate to within 10% for the GWB SNR and within 10% for the posterior standard deviations of the GWB parameters. Furthermore, these expressions are up to 100 times faster to evaluate than Monte Carlo simulations. We conclude that these results provide a highly efficient and precise method for estimating GWB SNRs and posterior uncertainties, which is particularly beneficial for conducting extensive parameter space analyses.

We examine the second species particle within the asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP) initiated at the origin, specifically analyzing the velocity distribution $p(v,t)$ as time $t$ advances. By utilizing the distribution's representation as an integral over a specific region in the complex plane, we derive an asymptotic form valid for large times. This derivation leverages the connection between $p(v,t)$ and the distribution of the largest eigenvalues of random matrices of the corresponding chiral symmetry class. Our findings indicate that, after rescaling, the velocity distribution $p(v,t)$ remains invariant with respect to time. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this distribution is independent of the initial boundary conditions at ASEP's origins, a result that holds true even when the system's asymmetry parameter $\gamma$ approaches zero. In the limit of small $\gamma$, the distribution $p(v,t)$ aligns with the $t^{-1}$ power law predicted by hydrodynamic theory.

We present a methodology for estimating parameters within differential equation models by integrating data with biological plausibility constraints. Our approach reformulates the parameter estimation challenge as a mixed-integer optimal control problem, utilizing mixed-logic piecewise continuous functions to encode specific biological knowledge. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through an application modeling the dynamics of SARS-CoV-2 infection, specifically employing a SIRV model fitted to viral load trajectories from a single patient.

We investigate the equilibrium properties of linearly confined Majorana fermions subjected to an external linear potential, $V(x) = \lambda |x|$. By employing the Feynman-Kac formula, we derive an exact expression for the density matrix and compute both Shannon's entropy and von Neumann's entropy. Our findings reveal that Shannon's entropy adheres to a universal scaling law dependent solely on the dimensionless parameter $\beta\lambda l$, where $l$ represents the system size and $\lambda$ defines the strength of the confinement. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the entanglement entropy for a bipartite system partitions linearly with subsystem size, exhibiting a characteristic logarithmic divergence at the boundaries.

Systems are increasingly utilized to support human tasks involving the identification and resolution of acronyms, a process where a term is first encountered in its full form and subsequently recognized by its abbreviated acronym. Because acronyms often remain ambiguous across different writing domains, these tools must effectively disambiguate them by identifying the corresponding full terms. This paper introduces a new approach to the automatic acronym-disambiguation task, where systems receive a corpus of text containing both acronyms and their full forms, along with instructions to generate mappings between them. We evaluate our method on three datasets of varying complexity, demonstrating that our system successfully disambiguates a substantial number of acronyms. Furthermore, we compare our results against human-generated disambiguation lists, showing that our approach achieves a high degree of agreement with human data.

We introduce an effective non-rigid pendulum model that captures the dynamics of atom-molecule conversion, including the emergence of system instabilities. By utilizing this framework, we identify the critical parameters determining the transition from stable atoms to stable molecules and observe that the quantum pressure arising from the discrete nature of atoms significantly suppresses instability. Furthermore, this model facilitates the derivation of a simplified nonlinear Schrödinger equation, which accurately approximates the full many-body Gross-Pitaevskii equation under conditions where the interaction strength is sufficiently high.

DNA data storage systems encode digital information into DNA molecules using primers to facilitate read and write operations. The efficacy of these systems relies heavily on the design of these primers. In this study, we introduce a novel algorithm that generates storage partitions by optimizing primer pair configurations. Our approach divides the vast design space into manageable sections, enabling the efficient generation of high-quality partitions. We implemented this algorithm in a prototype system that allows for the creation of optimized partitions for existing DNA data stored in synthetic oligonucleotides. Experimental results indicate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques, delivering superior performance with significantly reduced computational costs.

The discovery of topological nodal lines in momentum space has recently attracted significant interest, yet their physical realization remains limited. This study demonstrates that topological line defects can emerge in both real and momentum domains within systems possessing broken translational symmetry, specifically those featuring a one-dimensional dimerized lattice with alternating unit-cell widths. We derive the conditions necessary for the formation of these structures and illustrate how they manifest in a specific model system. Our findings reveal that the nodal lines in momentum space are characterized by one-dimensional topological protection, distinguished by non-integer Chern indices and the presence of robust surface states localized at the material's boundaries. Furthermore, we show that these defects generate nodal points in real space, which exhibit robustness against perturbations and host states confined to the interfaces of sub-lattices within different crystallographic directions.

Brain tumor segmentation is a critical challenge in medical imaging, with significant implications for patient care. This study introduces a novel deep learning architecture designed to classify and segment Glioma tumors in MRI scans. The proposed model utilizes a ResNet-50 backbone enhanced with a multi-scale attention mechanism to capture both local and global contextual features. Furthermore, it incorporates a dual-pathway decoder to refine segmentation accuracy. The model was evaluated on the BraTS 2015 dataset, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance by achieving a Dice Coefficient of 0.814 for whole tumor (WT) segmentation, 0.729 for tumor core (TC) segmentation, and an accuracy of 0.858 in tumor classification.

We introduce a novel shadow calculation method that significantly reduces the work required by ray tracing by leveraging the fact that shadows are computationally inexpensive to determine via rasterization. Our approach involves tracing only one primary ray per pixel, which intersects a single common occluder geometry. This contrasts with traditional rendering, where rendering engines trace thousands of rays per pixel to handle complex self-occlusion. By deferring the calculation of secondary shadows to a post-process step, we achieve a substantial performance boost. Although shadows are often considered a minor rendering detail, our technique delivers a noticeable real-time frame rate improvement.

Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs) have recently demonstrated exceptional performance in numerous image processing tasks, surpassing traditional algorithms. In this study, we introduce a DCNN-based deinterlacing framework designed to effectively handle various interlacing artifacts. The proposed architecture utilizes two distinct sub-networks: one dedicated to generating progressive frames from interlaced input and another for generating regressive frames. By training these models on synthetic interlaced data derived from progressive sources, we achieve state-of-the-art results in both objective metrics and perceptual quality.

This study examines the neutron skin in semi-microscopic nuclear models, specifically focusing on the dependence of neutron and proton effective masses and the symmetry potential on the choice of the real nucleon effective mass. Our findings indicate that neutron skins are primarily driven by the reduction of nucleon effective mass at the nuclear surface, which significantly influences the symmetry energy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that varying the symmetry potential provides a mechanism to adjust the neutron skin thickness independently of the real nucleon effective mass. These insights offer valuable guidance for constructing semi-microscopic models, particularly regarding the necessity of incorporating a symmetry potential that depends on the nucleon effective mass.

This study introduces a novel methodology for estimating riverbed bathymetry by integrating sparse Doppler sonar velocity data with geophysical constraints. The core of this approach is Principal Component Geostatistical Analysis (PCGA), which functions as a kriging technique constrained by principal component analysis. PCGA leverages the spatial correlation patterns inherent in extensive velocity datasets to interpolate missing values at a high resolution. By applying this interpolation to a dense grid, the method enables the efficient estimation of bathymetry through an inversion of the advection-diffusion equation, utilizing the known relationship between velocity and depth. Validation against field measurements from the Mississippi River demonstrates that this approach yields accurate bathymetric reconstructions, outperforming traditional Doppler-based methods in both precision and computational efficiency.

High Dynamic Range (HDR) imaging is essential for capturing scenes with extreme brightness variations, yet automatic High Dynamic Range (HDR) acquisition remains difficult because of the wide range of possible exposure values. This paper introduces a novel method for automatically selecting exposure levels for HDR creation by analyzing the local brightness of a scene. The proposed approach relies on a single low-exposure image to identify bright areas and a single high-exposure image to identify dark areas, determining the necessary exposure range based on these findings. The technique is straightforward to implement, requiring only a few camera settings and minimal post-processing. Experimental results indicate that this method is easy to deploy, robust, and effective in generating high-quality HDR images.

This work introduces a comprehensive survey on the emerging field of causal deep learning, addressing the intricate challenge of organizing a rapidly expanding array of methodologies. We categorize these approaches into a structured taxonomy based on the specific causal assumptions they incorporate and the corresponding causal models they represent. By organizing research according to these assumptions and models, this framework not only clarifies the landscape of causal deep learning but also aids in identifying promising avenues for future investigation.

This study introduces a novel, non-invasive temperature sensing technique for industrial reactors by leveraging the temperature-dependent proton resonance frequency (PRF) shift observed in water. The method relies on measuring PRF shifts using a standard radiofrequency (RF) coil, eliminating the need for additional hardware. The developed algorithm utilizes a pre-established PRF-temperature calibration curve to convert raw PRF data into temperature readings. The algorithm was validated using experimental results from a reactor test, demonstrating its accuracy and reliability. The results indicate that the proposed method achieves a measurement accuracy of approximately ±1.5 °C.

This paper presents a new proof of the Madsen-Weiss theorem, a foundational result in stable homotopy theory that identifies the $H\mathbb{Z}_\ell$-cohomology of the special orthogonal group $SO_n$ over a field of characteristic zero (where $\mathbb{Z}_\ell$ denotes the ring of $\ell$-adic integers). The approach relies on demonstrating the existence of a $\mathbb{Z}_\ell$-action on the relevant space of sections, thereby applying the $\mathbb{Z}_\ell$-theorem.

This study examines the Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) preconditioner for the nonconforming Crouzeix-Raviart finite element method applied to second-order elliptic problems with discontinuous coefficients. We derive BDDC preconditioned BDDC system eigenvalue and condition number bounds that explicitly feature the coefficient values and the mesh geometry. These findings demonstrate that the BDDC preconditioned system maintains a uniform condition number with respect to both the mesh mesh size and the discontinuity of the coefficients. Numerical experiments are included to validate these theoretical outcomes.

We examine $N\times N$ symmetric matrices $X_N$ composed of independent matrix entries that possess zero means and uniformly bounded absolute moments of all orders. We establish that, both in probability and almost surely, these matrices exhibit a limiting spectral distribution as $N \to \infty$. Specifically, we derive the Stieltmesth equation for the moment generating function of this distribution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the limiting eigenvalues of $X_N$ converge to those of a specific deterministic symmetric matrix $H_N$ featuring independent entries with identical marginal distributions, provided these match the required independence and moment conditions.

Background music generation is essential for creating compelling multimedia content, such as news and advertisements, by significantly enhancing the viewer's experience. We introduce a new framework that automatically produces audio tracks synchronized with video sequences, leveraging pre-existing music datasets. Our framework operates in two stages: initially, it learns to analyze the emotional tone of video footage and corresponding music through a dual-stream architecture that processes both visual and auditory inputs. Subsequently, it learns to generate audio by translating the extracted emotional features into appropriate tracks. Experiments using the Emotion-Synchronized Background Music Generation Dataset demonstrate that our model outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

Gradient masking represents a significant security vulnerability in neural networks, where attackers can exploit the fact that certain inputs prevent gradients from reaching specific parameters. Although various metrics exist to measure this phenomenon, they often yield conflicting results and lack a unified framework for evaluating different models. In this paper, we propose a novel, interpretable metric grounded in information theory. By quantifying the information contained within the gradient masking phenomenon, our approach offers a consistent method for assessment that enables meaningful comparisons across diverse neural network architectures.

This study examines the acoustic scattering of a plane wave by a microscopic annular ring metamaterial composed of Helmholtz resonators, with a specific focus on the influence of thermoviscous losses. By applying asymptotic analysis to the Navier-Stokes and energy equations, we derived asymptotic expressions for acoustic scattering that account for these losses. Our findings indicate that while the primary contribution of thermoviscous losses occurs within the narrow neck of the resonators, thermal losses dominate over viscous losses in this region. We further developed an asymptotic model for the complex effective acoustic impedance of the metamaterial, which aligns well with numerical simulations and experimental data. Additionally, we analyzed the acoustic transmission spectrum, demonstrating that incorporating these losses into the design framework allows for the creation of highly selective, narrow-band acoustic filters.

We examine the impact of Gaussian diffusion under conditions of both correlations and heterogeneity. Our findings indicate that these factors can invalidate standard Gaussian assumptions, resulting in deviations from the expected quadratic growth of the mean squared displacement (MSD). We introduce a generalized Gaussian framework incorporating these elements, which accurately fits experimental data from tracer particles in biological fluids. Additionally, we demonstrate that these correlations can be extracted from the observed dynamics through a maximum likelihood estimation approach.

This study examines the dynamics of a single photon confined within a low-loss, small-mode-volume microring resonator. We analyze how a photon's own state and the states of multiple external photons influence its evolution. By analyzing the resonator's Hamiltonian, we demonstrate that in identical counterpropagating modes, cross-phase modulation is twice as strong as self-phase modulation. Furthermore, we show that for such a one-photon system, the Hamiltonian effectively decomposes into two independent components: one acting on the photon's internal degrees of freedom and another governing its internal versus external state. These insights are utilized to define a novel entangling gate for a single photon's internal state and its external position. Additionally, we illustrate that the resulting dynamics yield a pure dephasing process for any multi-photon state.

This paper examines control systems governed by bounded controls and discontinuous feedback, with a specific focus on how control bounds influence trajectory dynamics. We illustrate the phenomenon of "chattering"—where trajectories oscillate rapidly around a set—by analyzing systems with one-dimensional unbounded controls. Furthermore, we introduce a class of control systems featuring bounded controls and feedback that is discontinuous only along specific trajectories, demonstrating that chattering can occur for every trajectory within this category.

This study introduces a multiscale enhanced Super-Resolution Generative Adversarial Network (MSR-SRResGAN) to elevate the fidelity of direct numerical simulation (DNS) data for turbulent channel flow at multiple Reynolds numbers. By integrating the model's multi-scale modules with the original MSR-SRResGAN architecture, the proposed method achieves a more robust reconstruction of DNS data. The results indicate that the proposed model outperforms the original MSR-SRResGAN across different Reynolds numbers, with the performance gap widening as the Reynolds number increases. The study concludes that the proposed model effectively reconstructs DNS data with minimal loss, regardless of Reynolds number variations.

This work presents a pedagogical demonstration of the discrete nature of electromagnetic field energy quantization. By employing the semi-classical Larmor formula to calculate the radiation power of an electron in a circular Bohr orbit, we derive the intensity ratio between the H$\alpha$ and H$\beta$ transitions of the Balmer series. Using this result, we subsequently derive Planck's law for blackbody radiation. This derivation confirms that the discrete energy levels of an atom interacting with a classically treated radiation field are sufficient to produce the discrete "quanta" of the full quantum electromagnetic field, thereby explaining the discrete frequencies observed in the hydrogen spectrum.

Confidence is a critical factor in the deployment of deep neural network (DNN) classifiers, yet traditional classifiers often lack the ability to express uncertainty regarding their predictions. This paper introduces a novel framework for enhancing confidence in DNN classification by integrating a new loss function with a specific regularization term. This regularization enforces a soft margin between the decision boundary and the decision regions associated with incorrect classes. We demonstrate that this approach yields a more robust and effective decision boundary compared to those generated by standard methods. Experimental results on three distinct datasets confirm that this proposed framework surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art decision boundary techniques.

Introducing MuJoCo Curriculum, a standardized framework designed to assess reinforcement learning (RL) methods in environments with varying levels of difficulty. This framework enables controlled modifications to curriculum parameters, facilitating rigorous evaluation of RL algorithms' adaptability to curricular shifts and their ability to generate effective curricula autonomously. We demonstrate the framework's utility by analyzing key aspects of curriculum design, including difficulty definition, dynamics, and generation mechanisms. Furthermore, we show how it offers a consistent basis for comparing RL methods through diverse benchmark tasks within the system.

Dynamic and complex business processes often undergo significant behavioral shifts over time, necessitating a modeling approach capable of capturing these dynamics. This paper introduces the concept of DCR graphs, which represent temporal process behavior through three complementary dimensions: control, data, and communication. We propose a novel algorithm that analyzes event logs to automatically construct DCR graphs. Furthermore, we present a new formalism for defining temporal process patterns based on these graphs. Our approach is evaluated using a real-world case study of the German tax office, demonstrating that DCR graphs can effectively mirror actual process behavior. Finally, we show that the proposed temporal pattern definitions are sufficiently expressive to account for observed behavior variations throughout the lifecycle of a process.

We offer a novel approach to comprehending the phenomenon of reentry in light localization and delocalization within quasiperiodic optical lattices. By applying a new analytical method to the tight-binding model, we derive an exact, closed-form solution for the Lyapunov exponent. This finding allows us to qualitatively grasp the reentrant transition by analyzing the interplay between quasiperiodicity and the system's boundary conditions. Furthermore, we derive an exact formula for the transmission coefficient of a finite quasiperiodic chain, which serves as a direct indicator of the transition behavior.

Liger is a distributed, in-memory relational database designed for big data environments, designed to integrate with the PetaData Reduction System (DRS) to leverage the Apache Spark framework. This design allows DRS to handle data reduction tasks, enabling Liger to concentrate on query processing. This paper describes the implementation of Liger, detailing how it utilizes DRS to manage data reduction and outlining its query processing mechanisms, which include the integration of a novel, parallelized version of the Magic algorithm for efficient data aggregation. Experimental results indicate that Liger significantly outperforms other Spark-based database systems in QPS and execution times when handling queries involving large volumes of data.

Imaging systems are susceptible to spatial entanglement arising from their limited resolution, a phenomenon quantified by the von Neumann entropy of the reduced state of a single photon. We demonstrate that this entanglement scales linearly with the squared inverse of the resolution limit, specifically $S \sim N_{\text{modes}}$, where $N_{\text{modes}}$ represents the count of linearly independent modes within the resolved region. Crucially, this linear relationship persists regardless of the specific linear transformation applied to the incoming field or the particular inter-pixel correlations of the detector. Furthermore, we introduce Schmidt number as a practical metric to characterize the entanglement of pure bipartite quantum states. Our findings indicate that for states generated by imaging systems, the Schmidt number approximates $N_{\text{modes}}$ and serves as a robust indicator of the degree of spatial entanglement.

This paper offers a survey of the Satake compactification, contrasting its geometric and Hodge-theoretic aspects with those of the Borel-Satake and other similar compactifications. We examine the construction of the Satake compactification from both geometric and Hodge-theoretic perspectives, while also exploring the Satake isomorphism and its implications.

The sudden onset of bistability in population dynamics can be anticipated by identifying specific bifurcation conditions. This study investigates the impact of a sudden, asymmetric mortality event on a prey-predator system governed by the Leslie-Gower model, focusing on how it influences bistability and the occurrence of abrupt dynamical transitions. By analyzing the model's nullclines and nullcline intersections, we derive an analytical criterion for locating a transcritical bifurcation. Leveraging this condition, we predict the sudden onset of bistability and the associated shifts in population dynamics.

We utilize a sample of 1,000,000 galaxies from the SPARC database to examine the connection between rotation curves and the NUV-r color in order to understand the evolution of the star formation history across different galaxy types. Our analysis reveals a bimodal distribution in the NUV-r color versus $M_{*}$ plane, where the divide occurs at approximately $10^{9.5} M_{\odot}$. Galaxies exceeding this mass threshold display a steeper negative slope in the relation between NUV-r color and mass compared to those below it. Furthermore, we observe that the NUV-r color becomes bluer as the peak circular velocity ($V_{\rm max}$) increases for systems with $M_{*} > 10^{9.5} M_{\odot}$. This trend persists even when galaxies are grouped by their $V_{\rm max}$ ranges, showing that the NUV-r color generally steepens with increasing stellar mass within each $V_{\rm max}$ bin. Additionally, we find that the NUV-r color steepens with rising $V_{\rm max}$ specifically for galaxies with stellar masses greater than $10^{10} M_{\odot}$.

Sentiment analysis is a critical natural language processing task with wide-ranging applications. Although models often achieve high accuracy in the language they are trained on, their performance typically declines when applied to other languages. To address this limitation, this study investigates how to train a model in a target language using only labeled target data and unlabeled source data, assuming the availability of a pre-existing source model and parallel corpora. We propose a novel framework that leverages the similarity between source and target languages to enhance performance. Specifically, we introduce a method to generate pseudo-labels for unlabeled target data by utilizing the source model and an ensemble of multiple labeled data augmentation techniques. Furthermore, we develop a new ensemble strategy that incorporates both the original source model and an ensemble of augmented pseudo-labeled models. Experiments conducted on three English-Turkish parallel datasets demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

This paper introduces a new approach for verifying programs that utilize cache coherence protocols. The method relies on the concept of a "weakened" coherence model, which permits coherence violations that do not alter program outcomes. By applying this model, the technique effectively verifies correct programs while inserting the minimal necessary coherence fences. Furthermore, the authors present an innovative algorithm for determining the placement of these fences. The approach is implemented as a plugin for the VeriLith framework, which simulates coherent caches. Experimental results indicate that the method is practical, capable of verifying realistic code snippets, and achieves significant reductions in fence usage compared to existing state-of-the-art solutions.

We investigate subsets of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ that allow a bounded number of elements whose sum equals $k$, demonstrating that such subsets must contain non-trivial arithmetic progressions of length depending only on $k$. Furthermore, we establish quantitative versions of these findings, including both inverse theorems and stability results.

This work offers a density characterization for fractional Brownian motion with dimension $d \geq 1$ and Hurst parameter $H \in (0,1)$. Specifically, for any Borel subset $E \subset \mathbb{R}^d$, there exists a non-trivial Hölder-continuous version of the density $\{B^H(t), t \in \mathbb{R}^d\}$ with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^d$ if and only if the Hurst parameter satisfies $H < 1 - \frac{d}{\dim_H(E)}$, provided the Hausdorff dimension of $E$ is strictly less than $d$.

This study examines the semiclassical dynamics of the Henon-Heiles model, a classic system renowned for its chaotic behavior, with a specific focus on the emergence of chaos as energy increases. By utilizing the correspondence principle, we analyze how chaotic characteristics evolve in relation to the H\'enon-Heiles Hamiltonian's chaotic phase space volume. Our findings indicate that chaos emerges when the ratio of the chaotic volume to the total phase space volume reaches approximately $0.06$, a value consistent with results from full classical treatments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this phenomenon arises from the proliferation of chaotic orbits situated in the chaotic sea, which eventually permeate the entire accessible phase space volume.

This study aims to enhance the allocation of ICU resources for COVID-19 patients by analyzing the relationship between ICU admission and mortality. We developed a new model that integrates the severity of COVID-19 with ICU admission probability and mortality rates. Our approach utilizes a hierarchical Bayesian framework to analyze data from 1,000 patients across 100 U.S. hospitals. We identified a set of features relevant to ICU admission and examined their distribution among admitted and non-admitted patients. By analyzing the conditional distribution of these features given ICU admission, we derived an admission probability model. Furthermore, we constructed a mortality model by conditioning feature distributions on both COVID-19 severity and ICU admission status. Our results indicate that ICU admission is driven by a combination of specific features and general disease severity, and that mortality rates vary significantly based on both the feature profiles of admitted patients and their specific ICU-related characteristics.

Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) aims to identify objects and infer the semantic relations connecting them within an image. Although recent advancements have significantly improved proposal generation and relation classification, the field still lags behind human-level performance. In this study, we introduce Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), a novel strategy designed to enhance the optimization of negative samples in the proposal phase. BNPS ensures that positive and negative proposals are balanced in terms of their count and quality. Unlike previous methods that rely on rigid, hand-crafted rules for relationship definition, BNPS leverages the implicit knowledge of relations learned by the visual pre-trained backbone. By identifying high-confidence negative proposals based on the output scores of the pre-trained model, BNPS effectively captures these complex patterns. Furthermore, we developed a new, flexible criterion for defining negative proposals that accommodates various forms of relationship negation. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on the Visual Scenes Relation Detection (VSRD) benchmark.

In supervised action recognition, the primary obstacle is the substantial amount of training data required to achieve satisfactory performance. This paper introduces a novel data-efficient approach that leverages the inherent temporal dynamics of videos. The proposed method trains a recurrent neural network (RNN) as an implicit autoencoder on unlabeled video data, learning to compress long sequences into shorter representations by predicting subsequent frames from recent history. These condensed representations are then utilized for action classification with only a minimal set of labeled data. Experiments conducted on the HMDB51 and UCF101 datasets demonstrate that this technique achieves an error rate only marginally higher than state-of-the-art models, despite utilizing a training dataset approximately 100 times smaller.

This document outlines the design and implementation of a Content Addressable Parallel Processor (CAPP), which connects to a host via a PCI interface for data input/output. The CARCH architecture serves as the internal content-addressable parallel processor, featuring a content-addressable memory (CAM) that supports parallel search operations. This design enables the parallel extraction of specific data values from a large dataset based on matching criteria, thereby significantly accelerating data extraction speeds.

Galactic formation is significantly shaped by accretion streams, which introduce diverse gas with varying metallicities and angular momenta. While the internal dynamics of individual streams have been studied, the evolutionary role of their internal structures remains unclear. We analyzed the three-dimensional structures of twelve streams at redshift $z=1.5$ using the IllustrisTNG simulation. Our findings reveal that streams evolve through a process of self-interaction and merging, undergoing a transition from chaotic, turbulent states at early phases to more coherent, ordered configurations at later stages. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the internal structural evolution of these streams critically determines the chemical and kinematic properties of the resulting galaxies.

The Universal Texture Zero (UTZ) model serves as a minimal framework for neutrino mass generation, positing that neutrinos acquire mass through a single Yukawa coupling to a single Majorana mass eigenstate. This model predicts a specific neutrino mass hierarchy and predicts that the neutrinoless double beta decay ($0\nu\beta\beta$) rate is either completely absent or significantly suppressed. Consequently, the UTZ model establishes a direct, one-to-one correspondence between the neutrino mass scale and physical observables, including neutrinoless double beta decay, neutrino oscillations, and beta decay.

We introduce a novel framework that leverages weak supervision from a static program analysis to train neural models capable of generating code. This approach uses a teacher model to generate labels for a dataset of unlabeled inputs, which are then employed to train a student model. We specifically address the challenge of generating Java assignments from problem descriptions by utilizing a GPT-2 architecture. Our method incorporates a new loss function designed to integrate the logits from the neural network with the teacher model's predictions. Experiments indicate that this weak supervision strategy significantly boosts performance compared to training solely on synthetic data, yielding a 10.4% improvement in pass@1 scores over the baseline.

On November 7th, 2004, a significant X-class solar flare with a magnitude of X1.8 occurred, accompanied by a Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) directed toward Earth. This event triggered a geomagnetic storm that reached its maximum intensity on November 8th, 2004, with a Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) index of -139 nT. This study examines the evolution of coronal structures associated with the November 2004 X1.8 solar flare and the subsequent Earth-directed CME, which generated the -139 nT geomagnetic storm. Utilizing data from the Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory (STEREO) mission, researchers analyzed coronal images from both the Heliospheric Imager (HI-1) and HI-2 instruments. The analysis focused on the timing, speed, and spatial trajectory of the CME as it traversed the field of view of the STEREO/HI instruments. The study reveals that the CME was initially detected by STEREO/HI-1 on November 7th, 2004, at 11:00 UTC, with the event continuing through November 8th, 2004, at 11:00 UTC.
